title: No smiles as Chris O'Connell advances, while Aussie women's campaign ends
text:
Chris O'Connell and Adam Walton have made it four Australian men in the third round of the Cincinnati Master, while Talia Gibson's loss to Aryna Sabalenka left the women's draw without green and gold representation.

Gibson was beaten 6-2, 7-6(7/2) by the world number one in an hour and 52 minutes, while O'Connell and Walton joined Alex de Minaur and Rinky Hijikata in the round of 32.

But O'Connell was in no mood to celebrate after progressing thanks to an injury retirement by 11th-seeded opponent Casper Ruud.

The Australian qualifier picked up his fourth win in five days at the Masters 1000 tournament in what is proving his most profitable week of the season, but there were no smiles as he sympathised with Norway's three-time grand slam finalist on his concerning retirement after 64 minutes play.

Ruud had started well, moving into a 5-2 lead in the opening set, but the Sydneysider powered back to take the first set, sealing it 7-5 with an ace, as Ruud began to look in increasing discomfort with a back problem.

With Ruud leading the second set 2-1 on serve, the Norwegian world number 17 stretched for a wide serve and immediately decided enough was enough, going to the net to offer his hand to the Aussie.

Clearly with one eye on the US Open, where the main draw starts a week on Sunday, 2022 Flushing Meadows runner-up Ruud was not keen to take any risks.

For world number 129 O'Connell, it was the continuation of an excellent spell following his first-round victory over Poland's world number 68 Kamil Majchrzak.

He will next meet Brazilian teenage superstar Joao Fonseca, who defeated Botic van de Zandschulp 6-4, 7-6(7/2), and victory in that match would push O'Connell back to the verge of the world's top 100.

Talia Gibson's loss to Aryna Sabalenka leaves no Australian women in the Cincinnati singles draw. (Getty Images: Robert Prange)

Walton made it four Australians through to the third round along with Hijikata, who faces Jakub Mensik, and national number one Alex de Minaur, who meets British Wimbledon hero Arthur Fery.

Walton, the 27-year-old Queenslander currently ranked 98 in the world, overcame the 29th-seeded Peruvian Ignacio Buse 6-4, 6-3 in 72 minutes to set up a showdown with either American Ben Shelton, the eighth seed, or Jaime Faria of Portugal.

title: Victorian teachers vote in favour of new pay deal after months-long dispute
text:
Victorian teachers and education staff have voted yes to a revised pay deal from the state government, signalling an end to a protracted bargaining process that saw two strikes held.

The revised government offer, which was handed down last week, promises pay rises between 28.3 per cent and 32.4 per cent over four years, and a lump sum payment of $2,000 at the start of the agreement.

The accepted offer also includes improvements to working conditions, with guarantees to reduce the number of meetings teachers must attend and providing professional practise days.

Premier Ben Carroll has also pledged to fully fund public schools ahead of the November election, one of the union's key demands.

The Victorian branch of the Australian Education Union said 83 per cent of its members participated in a vote, with 79 per cent of those voting in favour.

A third 24-hour strike scheduled for Wednesday will now not go ahead. (ABC News: Toby Hussey)

In a post on social media, AEU Victorian branch president Justin Mullaly congratulated union members for securing the pay deal.

"Together we've been able to get a significant outcome that delivers real pay increases, real improvements to conditions and we got a commitment from the state government to deliver full funding for our schools," he said.

"Remember that there are more things that we need to do. We need to make our schools safer. We need to make sure the federal government delivers funding for school buildings and infrastructure and we need to make sure that state government delivers on their promise to fully fund our schools."

The agreement brings an end to months of protracted discussion, with statewide strikes held in March and July.

The acceptance of the pay deal comes just days before a third planned 24-hour strike was due to be held on Wednesday, which has now been cancelled.

A government pay offer in June was voted down by 58 per cent of teachers and education staff, against union recommendations.

The agreement will now proceed to a vote of all employees as required under the Fair Work Act.

title: New privately operated prison announced by NT government
text:
The Northern Territory government has announced plans for a new prison that will be built and operated by a private company.

The 1,200-bed men's remand and intake centre and 200-bed women's facility will be built adjacent to the existing Darwin Correctional Precinct (DCP) at Holtze, on Darwin's outskirts.

The correctional facility at Berrimah is set to be closed by the early 2030s.

The government said the men's prison would be delivered under the Public Private Partnership (PPP), whereby the private partner would "design, finance, build, operate and maintain the facility", while the women's facility will be delivered by government as a design and construct tender, and operated by the Department of Corrections.

At a press conference this morning, NT Treasurer Bill Yan said a business case for the privatised prison was completed by Deloitte and will be published as part of the expression of interest process, which will go out to tender over the next week.

The NT government has announced a new privatised prison for Darwin. (ABC News: Matt Garrick)

"It's very, very important to know that the business case for this has been extremely rigorous and involved information and input from stakeholders, both within corrections and from within industry," he said.

"There will be no cost to the Territory on construction and design — that cost will be borne by the proponent and there'll be no risk to the people of the Northern Territory."

Chief Minister Lia Finocchiaro said the corrections system had been neglected for a decade and was unable to keep up with demand.

"There will always be an increase in prisoner numbers and we need to have a correction system that does the job it needs to do," she said.

"What this does for Territorians is mean they do not have any up-front construction or financial risk for this build.

"Territorians would not start paying for the new prison until the day we put prisoners in it."

NT Corrections Minister Gerard Maley said the government had been developing the master plan for corrections over the past two years.

"The decision to invest in a remand and intake centre will mean up to 45 per cent of our prison population moves out of DCP into more appropriate accommodation and services, leaving sentenced prisoners to be managed at DCP and Berrimah to be closed," he said.

Corrections Commissioner Matthew Varley said the new private remand centre would remain under his "custody, control, coordination and direction".

Matthew Varley says the move will boost rehabilitation outcomes for prisoners. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

"All Corrections infrastructure, no matter who it is operated by, falls under my remit and responsibility so the community can rest assured that the quality and safeguards are high," Commissioner Varley said.

"This is an opportunity to build a correctional system designed for the future with better infrastructure, better prison management and better outcomes for community safety."

In a statement the United Workers Union condemned the CLP government's plan labelling it "one of the most reckless corrections policy decisions ever proposed in the Northern Territory".

Erina Early says privatisation is not about improving outcomes. (ABC News: Hamish Harty)

NT Secretary of the union Erina Early added that privatising the operation of the men's facility was "not about improving outcomes" but about "allowing private corporations to profit from incarceration".

"A prison is not a commercial opportunity," Ms Early said.

"The deprivation of liberty is one of the most serious responsibilities of government and should never become a profit-making exercise.

"Every dollar paid out as profit is a dollar not invested in correctional officers, rehabilitation programs, mental health services, prisoner education or community safety."

The NT government says the NT correctional system requires major investment. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

However, Commissioner Varley said examples in other jurisdictions indicated private prisons "can be part of a sustainable, integrated and effective system".

"I challenge the assumption that the system of privatised prisons in the state does not work," he said.

"We're not making any of the current jobs in the correction system private whatsoever."

The NT government expects the successful proponent to be contracted by the end of 2027, with the rest of the design and construction process expected to take about four years.

According to data from the Productivity Commission from February this year there are currently eight privately operated prisons in Australia, located across New South Wales, Victoria, Western Australia and South Australia.

title: Concerns for emergency response during rolling Telstra upgrades
text:
Telstra customers in regional Western Australia say the telco's decision to conduct week-long upgrades without providing backup services could hamper emergency responders in one of the state's most prolific rescue zones.

The town of Gnowangerup, 350 kilometres south-east of Perth, sits at the base of the Stirling Range in the state's Great Southern.

Gnowangerup, home to about 1,200 people, is one of WA's most profitable grain-producing regions, and popular year-round with tourists visiting Bluff Knoll and the Stirling Range National Park.

The town of Gnowangerup sits at the base of the Stirling Range, a popular spot for hiking and tourists. (ABC Great Southern: Andrew Chounding)

Last week, Telstra told customers to expect service outages from Friday, August 14, lasting up to eight days, with outages of up to eight hours a day as it upgrades its 4G and 5G networks.

The timing and duration of the upgrades have "frustrated" customers and come at a time when the telco's regional service was facing increased scrutiny.

It has also raised concerns in Gnowangerup that first responders may be unable to muster volunteer crews effectively in an emergency.

Mandy Hanna, who is with the SES, is concerned the length of the outage could disrupt rescue operations. (ABC Great Southern: Andrew Chounding)

Emergency concerns

Gnowangerup State Emergency Service (SES) manager Mandy Hanna said its volunteers were often the first to respond to a road crash or distress call on Bluff Knoll.

"We're quite busy in the Stirling [Range] so if we can't be contacted at all we're not going to know if anything's happening," she said.

"My main concern is because we have that road crash capability, this is affecting people's lives."

Mandy Hanna says first responders and volunteers rely on mobile phones to coordinate their movements in an emergency. (ABC Great Southern: Andrew Chounding)

Ms Hanna said she had a personal Starlink satellite but stressed most SES members relied heavily on mobile phones to coordinate their movements in an emergency.

"Worst case, we can't be contacted for a road crash, and someone loses their life because we just don't know," she said.

"It's the same with St John's Ambulance [volunteers]; if we can't be contacted, we don't know."

Telstra is working to upgrade 4G and 5G services in the region. (ABC Great Southern: Andrew Chounding)

A Telstra spokesperson apologised for the inconvenience and confirmed the planned upgrades would not impact NBN, Satellite internet services, landline services, or mobile coverage from other providers.

They said calls to Triple Zero (000) would connect to another mobile network, if available.

"We're sorry for the disruption, but unfortunately this work is what's required to upgrade mobile connectivity in the area," they said.

"The team have planned this to minimise disruption as much as possible."

Darren Robertson says eftpos has been largely unusable since the service disruption. (ABC Great Southern: Andrew Chounding)

Business taking IOUs

The impact is being felt by some businesses in the town, including Darren Robertson, who owns the town's only cafe.

He said the outages of up to eight hours coincided with his opening hours, making his eftpos system unusable.

And with the ATM next door out of money, he said the cafe had been taking IOUs and hoping customers would return to pay.

Darren Robertson is taking IOUs from locals, but cannot serve tourists from out of town. (ABC Great Southern: Andrew Chounding)

"Yesterday it never worked at all … This morning it was on until about eight o'clock, and then it went off," he said.

" The locals are fine, but it's impacting my business because we've got people coming through that are from out of town, and a lot of people don't carry cash these days. "

Mr Robertson, who also uses a Starlink satellite at home, said he was considering replacing his Telstra service at the shop with another satellite to avoid future blackouts.

He also asked why Telstra could not use similar technology to maintain services for customers while the network was down.

"It goes to show how much we rely on Telstra, but I don't know why they couldn't set up a little portable tower or something while they do work on this big one," he said.

David Nicholson says Telstra's planning of the upgrades has been frustrating for customers. (ABC Great Southern: Andrew Chounding)

Shire chief executive David Nicholson has strongly criticised Telstra's communication and planning, suggesting shorter outages would reduce the impact on the town.

"I think it's quite atrocious and really poor customer service," he said.

"There should be some plan where perhaps the outage wasn't so long during the day.

"I get they've got work to do, but eight hours, I mean, my goodness, it's just basically down tools if you rely heavily on Telstra."

Telstra says customers can continue to make calls and send texts during the upgrades by switching on wi-fi calling, which requires access to a wi-fi source.

title: Broken zips, sleeve sewn shut: Union raises SA firefighter safety concerns
text:
Adelaide fire trucks have been grounded and some firefighting training temporarily cancelled, a union claims, amid concerns about the supply and maintenance of protective gear.

The United Firefighters Union has lodged a dispute in the SA Employment Tribunal, claiming the SA Metropolitan Fire Service (MFS) has failed to provide enough personal protective equipment (PPE) to its firefighters.

In documents lodged to the tribunal, the union argued the MFS had also failed to ensure its protective gear was "maintained, repaired, or replaced such that it continues to minimise risk to the worker who uses it".

"We seem to be faced with a massive failure of the PPE system in the MFS," Union acting secretary Peter Russell told the ABC.

"We've had items sewn on incorrectly, we've had things facing the wrong way, I think we had a sleeve sewn shut at one point in time.

" If that PPE is not working properly a firefighter could be exposed to severe injury or they could be killed. "

Photos provided by the union to the ABC show MFS gear with broken zippers and repairs.

A Metropolitan Fire Service firefighter wearing a coat with a faulty zipper. (Supplied)

Mr Russell said it was "impossible" to quantify how much MFS gear the union considered unsafe, as the service was unable to provide records.

"Even the newest gear… we have a very severe concern that the zips on those ensembles are faulty and [are] capable of coming apart during firefighting activities, exposing firefighters to risks of severe burns or death," he said.

The MFS said all of its "current operational structural firefighting" PPE met relevant industry standards and there was enough supply to ensure firefighters could safely respond to calls for help.

It said since 2023, the MFS had also been introducing new PPE.

"The safety of firefighters and the community is paramount," a spokesperson for the service said.

A faulty zipper on Metropolitan Fire Service personal protective equipment. (Supplied)

Concerns over laundering delay

Mr Russell said firefighters had told him "on many occasions" about their concern for how long PPE was taking to return from laundering.

He said delays of six weeks or longer had been reported to him and it had led to shortages.

"Firefighters are reluctant to put their firefighting gear in for laundering when it needs it, and risking using contaminated gear, because they do not trust that the system will return their gear to them," he said.

A lack of sufficient PPE is also to blame for fire trucks at the Elizabeth MFS station not being usable across the June long weekend, according to Mr Russell.

He said the union's own investigation had uncovered this was not an isolated incident.

"It became apparent to us that it wasn't an issue isolated to that station,"Mr Russell said.

" In effect, 30-year-old, 25-year-old sets of PPE had been reintroduced into circulation that never should have been. "

A MFS spokesperson did not comment on the Elizabeth example but said it was "not unusual" for a truck to be taken "offline" after it had responded to an incident.

"During this period firefighters and appliances are decontaminated, and equipment and PPE are restored and/or replaced as necessary," they said.

"Established processes are in place to ensure coverage is maintained and response times met during these periods."

The union claims that some MFS fire trucks have been grounded due to issues with PPE availability. (ABC News)

The spokesperson said in addition to individually-issued PPE, the MFS had reserves in several storage spaces "strategically located" across Adelaide.

"These caches are used to replenish PPE sent for decontamination and ensure firefighters continue to have access to fit-for-purpose protective equipment when responding to multiple incidents," they said.

"Older PPE sets identified in some caches have been removed."

'Temporary pause' on structural firefighter training

In a memo released earlier this month, and seen by the ABC, MFS chief officer Jeff Swann wrote that its Angle Park training centre "must not be used for training unless approval has been granted by the chief officer due to extenuating circumstances".

"This temporary pause will remain in place while the MFS considers the matters raised and determines any further steps that may be required," he wrote.

"Staff are reminded that recent MFS safety alerts have been issued regarding structural firefighting personal protective equipment, including alerts relating to the operation of LHD Sabre structural coat zippers and potential zipper separation."



Mr Russell said the shortage of PPE was partly to blame and he did not known when training would resume at the site.

"The situation has gotten so bad that they've had to close part of their training centre because they cannot operate it anymore safely," he said.

" If we're not running training, how are firefighters being equipped? "

A MFS spokesperson said a review was underway to ensure the training centre remained "safe and effective".

"Other training can continue to take place on site and this pause does not impact frontline emergency response," they said.

Emergency Services Minister Rhiannon Pearce said the state government continued to invest in firefighter equipment, training and resources.

"The Malinauskas Government has increased funding for emergency services including an extra $3.7 million for the MFS in 2024-25, compared to the previous financial year, and a further $589,000 to support the agency's large scale event response," she said.

title: Strokes are increasingly impacting young people and experts say the factors are complex
text:
Ben Murphy's first stroke took more than three days to be identified as he was shuffled between hospitals.

Aged 27 at the time, he puts the delayed diagnosis down to his age.

Calls for greater stroke awareness in the NT When then-38-year-old Alison Reidy woke up with a migraine, she never thought it would be a stroke. Now she's tyring to improve stroke awareness in the Northern Territory.

"It happened during COVID, so they were trying to get people in and out," he said, adding he was deemed fit for discharge after just 10 days.

Scans had also found a "hole" in Mr Murphy's heart, but doctors did not recommend he get it treated then.

Five years later, he had another stroke. This time far more severe and lead to a three-month stay in south-east Queensland hospitals.

"I completely lost my speech … and then I couldn't walk either because my right limbs, my hand, my leg, were just non-functional," the 33-year-old said.

" My life isn't really the same again, because this time, I'm still recovering. "

The severity of the second stroke prompted a procedure to close the heart opening.

Two years on, life back on his family farm in the Scenic Rim near the Gold Coast and a gradual return to activities like driving are helping him make strides towards independence.

Young stroke rates bucking the trend

Data from the Stroke Foundation shows more than 440,000 Australians were living with stroke as of 2023, with one in four strokes occurring in people of working age.

According to a review published by the World Stroke Organization (WSO) in January, the incidence of strokes amongst people aged under 55 has increased globally since the early 2000s, despite decreasing at older ages.

Stroke Foundation chief executive Lisa Murphy said it was a similar picture in Australia because prevention efforts still only targeted an older demographic.

"We've known for a long time that risk factors such as high blood pressure, high cholesterol, diabetes and a thing called atrial fibrillation, which is an irregular heartbeat, all contribute to a risk factor of stroke," she said.

Lisa Murphy says stroke symptoms are regularly being missed in emergency departments, by paramedics and other health professionals. (ABC News: Tara Whitchurch)

"And we know what to do about those … [however] that hasn't translated into young people yet, and I think one of the reasons why is a lot of those risk factors are actually silent."

Neurology professor Vincent Thijs from the Florey Institute of Neuroscience and Mental Health said the increased incidence in young people was limited to ischemic strokes, but the reasons as to why were not fully understood.

Ischemic strokes occur when a blood clot blocks an artery supplying blood to the brain and account for 80 per cent of all stroke events in Australia.

Many cases have no known cause

Professor Thijs said there had also been an increase in young stroke cases with no identifiable cause, known as cryptogenic strokes, with links to increased drug use, air pollution, longer hours at work, and delayed pregnancies.

Signs of stroke — use the FAST test Face: Has the mouth drooped?

Arms: Can they lift both arms?

Speech: Is their speech slurred?

Time: If you notice these signs, call Triple Zero (000) immediately. The Stroke Foundation also says regular health checks, exercise and a well-balanced diet go a long way to reducing the risk of strokes.

A Patent Foramen Ovale (PFO), a type of opening in the heart as with Mr Murphy, is another factor that has been associated with cryptogenic strokes.

Australian clinical trials suggest they are present in up to 50 per cent of cases in young people.

However, Professor Thijs said PFOs were common in healthy young people too and there was often no need to get them closed until a first-time stroke.

"More and better screening should occur after a stroke in the 18- to 60-year-olds as closure prevents a second stroke from happening if a PFO [with certain features] is identified," he said.

Gold Coast woman Ash De Cotta was "totally fit and healthy" before she suffered a brain stem stroke at the age of 35 and, two years on, still does not know why.

Ash De Cotta wants others to know stroke does not discriminate and to listen to their bodies. (ABC Gold Coast: Glenn Mullane)

"I had severe neck pain leading up to it, just out of the blue … and I had migraine with aura, which is where your vision sort of goes fuzzy, and that was about a month leading up to my stroke," she said.

" I did go to the doctors a few times, but I was just given painkillers and sent on my way. "

She ended up spending six months in hospital after suffering locked-in syndrome, a full-body paralysis caused by ischemic strokes.

Ms De Cotta said it was crucial people listened to their body and questioned unusual symptoms.

Different needs of young survivors

The Florey's Young Stroke Service is the sole dedicated service for young people, aged 18 to 55, recovering from a stroke but is only available in Victoria and South Australia.

Professor Thijs said there was a huge need for tailored support and funding to deliver such services Australia-wide.

"Younger people have different goals. They want to get back to work, they want to return to driving," he said.

Vincent Thijs says strokes in young people are still not the norm but having it on the radar is important. (Supplied)

"Our health system isn't particularly catered towards the needs of these younger stroke survivors, so that's why the impact is different and bigger in many respects."

Ms De Cotta agreed.

"Typically, people think older people have strokes, and that's not the case, and services do need to catch up with that," she said.

title: Data centres to be fast-tracked in NSW, despite community group pushback
text:
A new government initiative incentivises data centre builders to comply with freshly set guidelines if they want to fast-track their developments.

Builders will have to meet environmental and efficiency standards, impose no net cost to consumers and fund additional supply of water and energy.

They will also have to enhance local community infrastructure, invest in "future industries" and commit to skills training and support jobs.

In return the state government promises to assess their applications within 75 days.

19 more data centres are currently on the way in NSW. (ABC News)

'We have to replace a lot of old energy sources'

With more than 60 data centres already operating or under construction in NSW and 19 more in the planning and approval pipeline, the government said it was time to set regulations.

Treasurer Daniel Mookhey said the government had been working on the framework for more than a year.

"We are launching a nation-leading policy to make sure that rising data centre investment is matched with increased investment in renewable energy and water infrastructure," he said.

Mr Mookhey said under the new framework data centre builders would foot the bill for new clean energy, sparing Australian taxpayers.

Daniel Mookhey announced the new scheme on Monday. (ABC News)

"There's no doubt we have to replace a lot of old energy sources like coal fire power. We do and should replace that with clean, green, renewable power," he said.

" We want data centre builders to help pay their fair share, so it doesn't just fall to households to pick up the cost. "

Minister for Climate Change, Environment and Energy Penny Sharpe said applications would be "held to the highest possible standards in our environmental protections system".

"We will have the most stringent environmental standards," she said.

"By 2030, data centres could take up 11 per cent of energy needs in NSW. That's a challenge but it's also an opportunity for us to underpin greater investment in renewable energy investment into the future."

Penny Sharpe says the guidelines take environmental factors into consideration. (ABC News)

The framework trades compliance for speedy government assessments, but it does not set out penalties for builders that refuse the government's offer.

Mr Mookhey said builders that did not meet the standards could have their proposals rejected.

"Those data centre builders that choose not to comply with these guidelines will have to take the risk that their projects are going to get refused," he said.

"We're pretty clear that these are our expectations … any data centre builder that chooses not to comply with these standards will find themselves almost alone."

Data centres face backlash

A group of students and community organisers protested the increase of data centres around Western Sydney on Sunday.

Gokulan Gopal is a local community organiser who spoke at the protest calling for a moratorium on new AI data centre builds until the community is consulted and has a better understanding of the impacts of living next to these data centres.

Gokulan Gopal questions where the water is going to come from for new data centres. (ABC News)

"Where is the water going to come from? Where is the power going to come from? How are we going to manage the waste? When the outage happens, what kind of backups are they going to use?" he said.

" If they're going to consume that much power, what will happen to our power price? What will happen to our water price? So there is really some serious unanswered questions. "

Sophie Shanaaz represents a campaign called 'Stop the Slop' which opposes the expansion of data centres in Western Sydney.

"We're really focused on getting all these AI data centres out of our suburbs … eating our resources. We're not happy about it and we want to do something about it," she said.

"I live in very close proximity to one being developed and I feel that there is not enough regulation at the moment."

Mr Mookhey said he was aware of community concerns and believed the new regulations would address them.

"This technology is only going to have social license if people can see that there is a strong dividend for them and their children, as well as our state and our nation's future," he said.

"The principle that we're setting for today is really straightforward. Data centres that want to build in New South Wales need to bring power, not take it."

Builders who do not meet the fresh guidelines could have their proposals rejected. (ABC News)

Water usage addressed in guidelines

Under the new framework, data centre builders would need to show they were entering into power purchasing agreements with renewable energy providers.

"That means that if these data centre builders sign those contracts, it results in less bills for households," Mr Mookhey said.

Similar to energy consumption, data centres are also resource intensive when it comes to water usage.

Mr Mookhey said the guidelines addressed this by setting certain water usage efficiency standards and by incentivising data centre builders to invest in water infrastructure.

The Sydney suburb at risk of becoming a 'data centre wasteland' Sydney is in the middle of a data centre boom fuelled by the global AI race. In Lane Cove West and Ryde, residents and councils say they are the ones paying the price.

The framework will come with a water pricing review to be conducted by the Independent Pricing and Regulatory Tribunal (IPART), which would aim to "ensure water users on the network are protected and the impacts of drought and water scarcity are appropriately managed".

A new Office of AI will also be established to coordinate government investment in digital and AI assets to "ensure AI supports workers, strengthens capacity and is implemented responsibly across the public sector".

The new framework and Office of AI come into effect on Monday, while the IPART review might take longer.

title: After constant chopping and changing, Green goes 'back to what worked'
text:
Cameron Green has delivered for a shell-shocked Australian side to give himself breathing space at number five, leading captain Pat Cummins to predict a long stint in one position in the batting line-up.

Green's 104 in the second innings of the nine-wicket loss to Bangladesh in Darwin was his first in Australia and also broke an 11-innings run without passing the half-century mark.

The 27-year-old all-rounder has been heavily criticised in Australian cricket for not turning his undoubted potential into results.

But his knock in the loss means he leaves the Northern Territory as one of the only Aussie batters who can hold their heads high, with Cummins "not too sure" on the best course of action to turn things around before the second Test starts in Mackay on Saturday.

Shock loss to Bangladesh reveals Aussie cracks On paper, Australia's full-strength team should have wiped the floor with Bangladesh. But a lack of application to their Test match craft has left Australia vulnerable to teams that are driven to succeed in the longest format.

"We're always quite individual, everyone goes about it slightly differently, so coaches will work with each player individually," he said.

"I don't think there was a huge trend, everyone got out a little bit differently, but I think it's pretty clear it's not quite functioning as well as we'd like as a group.

"If we need to make some changes to our style, we've got a week or so, we better do it pretty quickly."

Cummins said before the Test that Green had been encouraged to "intimidate" and he did it the way he knows best, driving with commanding power and poise while accumulating runs at a steady rate without taking risks.

It is a method that has worked in Sheffield Shield cricket and he showcased why Test selectors have persevered with him despite the outside noise calling for his head.

Green's third Test century did not lead to a win but that was largely due to the failure of the rest of the order to stay with him in good batting conditions on the third and fourth days.

Australia will consider making changes to the underperforming top order for the second Test in Mackay that starts on Saturday, but Green will be one of the first picked.

"I'm sure he will get an extended run somewhere," Cummins said when asked if Green had tied down the number five position.

"I thought he was really impressive and controlled his innings. He looked in total command of his skills out there. He just needed one or two of us to bat alongside him."

Green and Steve Smith were the only Australian batters who could be happy with their output. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Green struggled in the last Ashes series, as many batters did, making just 171 runs at an average of 24.42 after being moved around from fifth to eighth in the order.

He earlier did a solid job on the West Indies tour, averaging 30.66 at first drop as the only member of the top three to average more than 20 across the three Tests.

"We obviously think very highly of Cam," Cummins said.

"The last Ashes series probably didn't go as well as he would have liked but before that on the West Indian tour he was probably our best batter in really tough circumstances when he was batting a little higher.

"It was great for him to go out there and show the rest of the world how good he is."

Quick hits as Bangladesh wraps up famous win Litton Das was wrong-footed behind the stumps, and Mehidy Hasan Miraz suffered a worse fate in front of them. Here are the quick hits from day four of the first Test between Australia and Bangladesh.

Green was fortunate in the final session on the third day when an inside edge off Taskin Ahmed grazed his leg stump on the way to the boundary.

The bails were not dislodged and the all-rounder dug in and made the most of his reprieve.

Green told Fox Cricket after his knock that he had approached his innings against Bangladesh like he used to do "back in the day".

"I think I've just been chopping and changing a little bit recently, so it's nice just to go back to what worked," Green said.

"It has been a long couple of months so it is nice to get a few rewards for it."

As for the critics, Green said it just came with the territory.

"I feel like there are always wolves when you are playing Test cricket. When you play for Australia, you always have to perform," he said.

title: Director faces investigations following Mundella collapse
text:
Creditors say they may not see a cent of the millions owed to them by collapsed West Australian dairy processor Mundella Foods and two other associated companies.

Mundella, Margaret River Dairy Company and The Cheeky Cow were put into liquidation this month.

Director Hayden Russell is facing investigations by liquidators at Mackay Goodwin following administrators' preliminary suggestions of insolvent trading and hundreds of potentially "unreasonable transactions".

Dairy farmer and Mundella Foods milk supplier Phil Hall told the ABC he was owed "enough money to buy a house" and expected to get nothing back from the liquidation.

Phil Hall says he is still owed hundreds of thousands of dollars by Mundella Foods. (Supplied: Facebook/Halls Family Dairy)

"I don't know what happened to Mundella, but I know this year we basically never got paid," he said.

"Myself and another dairy farmer, we both did the same thing, believing in this company.

"We wanted this to work because it was the only way forward for the future."

A trio of well-known dairy companies have collapsed after being put into voluntary administration a year ago. (ABC South West WA: Jon Daly)

The unpaid debt contributed to his family's recent decision to sell their farms at Wokalup in WA's South West and leave the dairy industry after six generations.

"I remember being three and running around this farm," Mr Hall said, choking back tears.

Do you know more about this story? Get in touch via email Daly.Jonathon@abc.net.au

Failed rescue plan

Mundella, Margaret River Dairy Company and The Cheeky Cow were put into liquidation on August 6, following the termination of a Deed of Company Arrangement (DOCA) put forward by Mr Russell in August last year.

Mr Hall is among the unsecured creditors still owed millions.

They were told they could see a potential return of 68 cents to the dollar under a rescue plan to sell the real estate portfolio of the companies under lease-back arrangements.

But administrators told the ABC the DOCA had been terminated as a result of Mr Russell's non-compliance with the terms of the deal.

It is not known what breach triggered the termination of the rescue plan.

Hayden Russell is facing scrutiny following the liquidation of the business and other associated companies. (Supplied: Kira Price)

A financial statement seen by the ABC shows more than $620,000 was paid from the administration accounts during the DOCA period for expenses, including administrator fees, trading costs and supplier payments.

Just under $13,000 remained when the deed was terminated.

There appears to have been no significant distribution of money to unsecured creditors.

The companies' property and remaining assets have been transferred to the mortgagee, Bowral Capital Pty Ltd.

Mr Hall said he held no ill-will towards Mr Russell, because he had initially paid dairy farmers 90 cents a litre for milk, compared to 76 cents offered by other processors.

"I'm not angry with Hayden because he was trying to do the right thing for the dairy industry," he said.

"None of the other milk companies were offering anything near the price he was offering, and nor are they trying to do anything for the farmers left in the industry."

Former Mundella Foods employee Mairee Wall is less forgiving.

Mairee Wall says the collapse of Mundella Foods "broke" her and other employees, who were once proud of the brand. (ABC South West WA: Jon Daly)

She said she was still owed about $10,000 of unpaid annual leave and superannuation.

Ms Wall worked as a pasteuriser at Mundella Foods' Mundijong manufacturing facility near Perth from 2012, well before the company was purchased by The Cheeky Cow, a company majority-owned by Hayden Russell.

"That's when things very quickly unravelled," she said.

"Things went drastically wrong. There was no protocol. There was just no structure."

Ms Wall said she was once proud of making the Mundella brand of yoghurt, which had previously won national awards.

"We put everything into it, and it really broke a lot of people, me being one of them, when things just fell apart and just so quickly," she said.

Thoroughbred industry reports named Hayden Russell as the buyer of the stallion God Has Spoken in November last year. (Supplied: OzRace)

Thoroughbred purchases

Industry reports and bloodstock sale records indicate Mr Russell expanded his involvement in WA's thoroughbred industry during the past year.

Thoroughbred Breeders WA reported in November last year that "Margaret River Dairy Company owner Hayden Russell" had purchased a stallion named God Has Spoken, and the ABC has confirmed that purchase agreement.

The dairy companies' assets and properties have been transferred to the mortgagee, Bowral Capital Pty Ltd. (ABC South West WA: Jon Daly)

Sale results on online horse auction site Magic Millions list a buyer identified as "Hayden Russell, WA" as purchasing five horses earlier this year.

There is no evidence in the administrators' reports linking Mr Russell's thoroughbred purchases, which had total costs of under $10,000, to the dairy companies' funds or to the transactions flagged for further investigation.

The ABC has contacted Mr Russell for comment.

Liquidators to investigate

In a report lodged with the corporate watchdog, administrators stated that the downfall of the companies was the combined result of "poor financial control/lack of records", "poor strategic management" and trading losses.

The liquidation process will involve further investigations of Mr Russell's duties as director.

Administrators flagged about 235 transactions worth more than $100,000 that may be considered "unreasonable director-related transactions" across the three companies.

The administrators also noted "sufficient evidence to suggest" Mundella had traded while insolvent from July 2024 and Margaret River Dairy Company from December 2023.

They estimated about $3.7 million in debt was incurred during that time, and said Mr Russell "may be personally liable for insolvent trading".

Administrators said preliminary findings had identified potential offences they intended to lodge with the corporate watchdog.

title: Live: NAB home lending decline led by investors, more loans 'on watch'
text:
Wall Street's recent rally came to a shuddering halt on Friday thanks to increased anxiety about the US failing to extricate itself from its Middle East quagmire and wilting consumer sentiment.

Even putting the 6% rise in global oil prices over the week to one side, US consumers are becoming increasingly jaded about their cost-of-living pressures.

The keenly observed University of Michigan's consumer sentiment survey came in at 51 points in August, below expectations of 54.5.

US retail sales data released on Friday also showed a surprising and sharp decline in consumer spending.

The data further reduced expectations of a Federal Reserve rate hike at next month's meeting.

US Treasuries fell on Friday, pushing the US dollar down and giving the Aussie dollar a lift to just under 71 US cents.

Wall Street's close showed all key indices, as well as the global MSCI, losing ground.

S & P 500: -0.2%

-0.2% Dow: -0.2%

-0.2% Nasdaq: -0.3%

-0.3% MSCI: -0.1%

The ASX looks like following that trend with futures trading on Saturday morning's close pointing to a 0.4% decline today.

Over the week the S & P 500 rose 0.4% while the ASX 200 fell 1.6%.

The S & P 500's slip from record highs was in part driven by selling in chipmakers such as Applied Materials, Broadcom and Intel.

European shares finished lower on Friday and snapped a four-week winning streak, as rising crude prices and renewed geopolitical tensions offset support from a resilient earnings season.

Oil prices continued to bubble up as there is no end in sight to hostilities in the Middle East.

Brent crude oil futures: +1.7% to $US88.52 a barrel

+1.7% to $US88.52 a barrel West Texas Intermediate crude futures: +1.4% to $82.40

Senior portfolio manager for fixed income at Federated Hermes, John Sidawi, told Reuters a puzzling feature of markets in recent months has been the growing disconnection between geopolitical uncertainty and asset price volatility.

"For now, markets appear willing to tolerate a significant amount of uncertainty without demanding higher risk premiums. However, this equilibrium is unlikely to be permanent," Mr Sidawi said. "A meaningful escalation in conflict or a clear path toward resolution could finally force investors off the sidelines, potentially triggering a much larger volatility response than current market pricing implies."

Gold is one beneficiary of the current situation, up almost 1% to $US4,390/ounce, its highest level since early June.

title: Aussie star Lani Pallister ends American GOAT's 16-year win streak
text:
Lani Pallister has toppled swimming legend Katie Ledecky for a second time in 24 hours to complete her stunning Pan Pacific championship campaign with a fourth gold medal.

The 24-year-old Pallister was under world-record pace for much of the race as she won the 800m freestyle final in eight minutes and 6.1 seconds from four-time Olympic champion Ledecky (8:07.26) in the American's signature event.

Ledecky's lone previous defeat in an 800m freestyle final since 2010 came in a small domestic event in February 2024 against Canadian superstar Summer McIntosh, making Pallister the first to beat her over the distance at an international meet.

"Today is the most nervous I've ever felt in my entire life. I was just so locked in and I've been really focused on what I want," Pallister said.

"The 800m is my favourite event. So to have the three titles this week and be just behind Katie in the 1,500 [is great but] … this is the one that I wanted."

Ledecky, who famously signed an autograph for a young Pallister a decade ago, telling her to "dream big", wrote on Instagram that she "can't help but smile about another incredible race with [Pallister]".

Ledecky (right) told a young Pallister to "dream big". (Getty Images: Maddie Meyer)

Pallister had beaten Ledecky to win the 400m freestyle gold a day earlier and took silver behind her great rival in the 1,500m free, as well as downed McIntosh to win the 200m free gold and also collect gold in the 4x200m free relay.

Australia's Dolphins well and truly flexed their middle- and long-distance muscle at the meet, two years out from the LA Olympics, with Sam Short also emerging with three individual gold medals after winning the men's 1,500m free to go with his 400 and 800 free titles.

Having beaten Ian Thorpe's 1999 Pan Pacs record to win the 400m, he erased another Australian legend's mark in the 1,500m.

His time of 14:33.97 was the sixth-fastest in history, breaking Grant Hackett's Australian record that had stood since 2001, and came a day after German teenager Johannes Liebmann smashed the world record at the European Aquatics Championships.

Loading Instagram content

"I am proud of my consistency," said Short, who also won the 400m, 800m, and 1,500m titles at the Commonwealth Games late last month.

"I've gone five well sub-15-minute swims now, so if I can do that here my average come Olympics, world championships, all I need to do is be my average and be contending for some podium places."

Adding to a strong final day for Australia, Zac Stubblety-Cook went from fourth to first in the 200m breaststroke final, winning in 2:08.09 from American Josh Matheny.

And countryman Jamie Jack won the 50m freestyle gold in a championship record of 21.35 as American Jack Alexy took silver in 21.42.

"It's awesome. That's the best I could ask for," Jack said.

American Kate Douglass lowered her own world record in the 50m free twice, winning the final in 23.19.

Douglass capped a busy night by anchoring the US women to a dominant victory in the 4x100 medley relay in a championship record time of 3:50.43, with Australia second in 3:55.09.

The US men won from Australia in the 4x100 medley relay.

Australia finished the four-day meet with a medal haul of 15 gold, 11 silver and nine bronze, behind only the US haul of 19, 22 and nine.

title: Batemans Bay ED closing despite population hitting 80k over summer
text:
When Christine Hayes suffered a stroke at her Surfside home on the New South Wales South Coast every minute counted as she waited for medical help to arrive.

An ambulance came and took her to the Batemans Bay Hospital's emergency department where she says she received treatment within 20 minutes.

"The nurses and doctors there saved my life," she said.

But that very emergency department where she says her life was saved will close its doors early next year, despite the region being a popular holiday destination with a growing population.

The decision to close the Batemans Bay Hospital and its emergency department was made when the New South Wales government committed to building the new Eurobodalla Regional Hospital in Moruya — 30 kilometres away.

Ms Hayes has ongoing health issues and credits the staff at Batemans Bay emergency department with saving her life. (ABC News: Penny Travers)

"My heart is also an issue now. I worry that if I have a heart attack, or if I have another stroke, and have to go to Moruya, it's going to be too long before I get there," Ms Hayes said.

The additional travel time to reach an emergency department is what also worries local GP Dr Andrew Gibson.

"My concern is that there's almost 20,000 people in Batemans Bay, swelling to almost 80,000 between Christmas and Easter, and these people will have to go 30 kilometres for urgent medical treatment," he said.

" I think that is a dangerous thing and it doesn't have to be if we had maintained an emergency facility in Batemans Bay. "

Batemans Bay District Hospital will close next year when the new regional hospital opens in Moruya. (ABC News: Penny Travers)

Additional travel time

The new level four Eurobodalla Regional Hospital is being built south of the Moruya township on the Princes Highway, and will replace both the existing level three Moruya and level two Batemans Bay hospitals.

Being a level four hospital, the $330 million facility will offer a higher level of care and wider range of services than the existing hospitals, including a paediatric ward and intensive care unit, and is expected to reduce the number of patients that need to be transferred to other hospitals like Canberra and Bega.

The new Eurobodalla Regional Hospital is expected to open early next year. (ABC News: Jacinta Counihan)

The government says the site was chosen in part for its centrality within the shire, which stretches 110 kilometres along the coast from South Durras in the north to Narooma in the south.

Both NSW Health Minister Ryan Park and local member for Bega Michael Holland say it will only take an ambulance 15 to 20 minutes to travel from Batemans Bay to the new hospital.

"Health Infrastructure consulted Transport for NSW on the location of the new Eurobodalla Regional Hospital," Mr Park said in a statement.

"The site was selected with existing roads and traffic taken into consideration.

"We are working closely with NSW Ambulance to build on our already strong processes ahead of the new hospital opening – ensuring timely access to emergency medicine and care wherever it is needed in the Eurobodalla."

Batemans Bay emergency department will close next year. (ABC News: Penny Travers)

But community action group Don't Close Batemans Bay ED questions whether the trip can be done in that time.

"These guys are out of touch," group founder Peter Ryan said.

"We've actually measured it under the lights and sirens situation from the Batemans Bay CBD to the new hospital site – it's 29 minutes at best."

'Bridge is a bottleneck'

There is only one bridge crossing the Moruya River into the north of the town, and during busy holiday periods traffic can be seen backing up over the bridge and along the Princes Highway — sometimes stretching for kilometres.

The NSW government has long-term plans to build a bypass around Moruya and a preferred route was announced in July 2024. But funding has yet to be allocated for the project, with construction costs now estimated to be more than $1.7 billion.

There is only one bridge crossing the Moruya River into the north of the town. (ABC News: Penny Travers)

"The bridge is a bottleneck," Dr Gibson said.

"Even with a clear run, it's 30 minutes [from Batemans Bay].

"Nobody could ever believe that treatment in the back of an ambulance by paramedics, no matter how well trained they are, is better than treatment by emergency-trained doctors in an emergency department."

Dr Andrew Gibson is especially holds concerns for Batemans Bay's elderly residents. (ABC News: Penny Travers)

Dr Gibson is particularly concerned for those living north of the Batemans Bay bridge in areas such as Nelligen.

"In emergency medicine there's a thing called the golden hour, and that's the most important time in an urgent medical problem," he said.

" What happens in the first hour, it very often may decide life survival or not surviving. So that's why it's important people ... can be treated immediately. "

But Dr Holland does not see the additional travel time or congestion on the bridge as being an issue for Batemans Bay residents.

"Ambulances are allowed to exceed the speed limit and ... they're used to handling traffic obstructions," he said.

"I spent 23 years of my career being on call for either Batemans Bay or Moruya District Hospital, and I can tell you that the majority of that time there is no traffic [on the bridge]."

Holiday-makers and elderly residents

More than 19,300 people live in greater Batemans Bay, with the population swelling to some 80,000 over summer.

And with planning submissions currently before council for more apartment complexes and holiday units, and hundreds of new homes under construction in areas like West Rosedale, the Batemans Bay greater population is only expected to grow.

The greater Batemans Bay population swells to more than 80,000 over the summer months. (ABC News/Penny Travers)

Eurobodalla Shire mayor Mathew Hatcher said in recent years, tourists had been frequenting the region more and more.

"We're seeing that [tourist] swell more year round as well. It's not just in those summer weeks," he said.

"Weekends now, we're seeing a lot of our Canberran friends coming down the mountain."

Mathew Hatcher says more tourists are visiting the region year round, particularly from Canberra. (ABC South East NSW: Fatima Olumee)

Batemans Bay also has a large elderly population many of whom, Dr Gibson said, had chosen to retire in the area thinking there was a hospital close by.

He treats dozens of patients at three aged care facilities, and said travel to and from Moruya would be difficult for many elderly residents.

"Taxis [from Moruya] are prohibitively expensive. A lot of the older people don't drive. Certainly a number of them wouldn't drive to Moruya," Dr Gibson said.

18,000-strong petition

Dr Gibson and Ms Hayes are far from the only ones concerned, with some 18,000 people signing a petition to keep the Batemans Bay ED operational once the new Eurobodalla Hospital opens.

"We were completely blindsided," Mr Ryan, who helped organise the petition, said.

" The community didn't know they were losing their ED as part of the new hospital. "

Peter Ryan is pushing for the Batemans Bay emergency department to remain operational once the new hospital opens next year. (ABC News: Penny Travers, PENNY TRAVERS)

The petition was presented and discussed in the NSW Legislative Assembly but Mr Ryan said it had not progressed from there.

"The [government] is playing Russian roulette with lives. Lives will potentially be lost," Mr Ryan said.

"It's a big population and we need to have some form of emergency department ... so people can be triaged in the first instance, life saved, and then they can get [further] care after."

More than 19,300 people live in greater Batemans Bay, with the population more than tripling over the summer months. (ABC News: Toby Hemmings)

The Eurobodalla Shire Council has also voted unanimously to lobby the state government against closing the ED, but Mr Hatcher said the government was steadfast in its decision.

"Ultimately, it's been made pretty clear by the state at all levels from the Premier down that they will not be changing their tune," he said.

'Better, definitive care'

Dr Holland, who worked as an obstetrician in the region for more than 20 years before entering politics, has rejected the assertion that lives could be lost because of the ED closure, and said the new hospital would in fact provide better care.

"The emergency department in itself will have more treatment spaces compared to the [current] two emergency departments combined," he said.

"It's better care for people to have definitive care rather than present to a level two hospital where not all facilities are available, only to be then transferred to another hospital."

Premier Chris Minns and Bega MP Dr Michael Holland inspected the site of the new Eurobodalla Regional Hospital earlier this month. (ABC News: Mikayla McGuirk-Scolaro)

Dr Holland said the region could only have a higher care level four hospital service by combining the existing ED presentation of both Moruya and Batemans Bay.

"By keeping two hospitals open, you can't achieve that greater provision of care because of the challenges in retaining staff and workforce," he said.

The new level four Eurobodalla Regional Hospital will have the shire's first paediatric ward and ICU. (ABC News: Jacinta Counihan)

Dr Holland also noted that Batemans Bay now had a Medicare-funded Urgent Care Clinic with extended opening hours.

"People from south of Narooma will have to travel distances to get to this new level four hospital and people from Batemans Bay will have to travel a distance," Dr Holland said.

title: Licence loss, fines for companies hosting migrants in shoddy housing
text:
Labour hire companies that house migrant workers in substandard accommodation will risk losing their licence as part of a new crackdown.

The Victorian Labour Hire Authority has launched new licence conditions after a series of cases in which migrant workers were housed in poor conditions.

The authority, which works to prevent the exploitation of labour hire workers, brought in the conditions for businesses that provide housing for their workers.

The conditions have been put in place for providers in industries such as horticulture and meat processing, which have high rates of worker exploitation.

In addition to losing their licences, businesses that do not comply face fines of more than $160,000.

The Labour Hire Authority is increasing accommodation inspections. (ABC News: Justine Longmore)

The authority's director of intelligence, compliance and enforcement Erin Barlow said the changes were aimed at protecting vulnerable workers.

"We know that when accommodation is tied to employment, workers can feel unable to complain because they can be fearful of losing both their job and their housing," she said.

"These workers are especially vulnerable to exploitation."

Ms Barlow said the new conditions were in response to substandard worker accommodation the authority had seen.

In December 2025, the authority found 22 migrant workers were housed in unsanitary conditions in a single home and a granny flat in Gippsland.

Mould, sewage and overcrowding Migrant workers in Victoria's east were made to pay $190 a week to their employer for overcrowded, mouldy accommodation.

The accommodation in Warragul, about an hour east of Melbourne, had sewage pooling in the front yard and black mould covering doors, windows, ceilings and curtains.

"In that case, we saw some of the worst accommodation that we had experienced," Ms Barlow said.

"Providers can expect to see us out and about inspecting that accommodation more now that we are introducing these conditions.

" Accommodation is a clear focus for the Labour Hire Authority in the next year. "

'Not fit for an animal'

Migrant Justice Institute co-executive director Bassina Farbenblum has welcomed the change.

Bassina Farbenblum says unhygienic, overcrowded accommodation can harm workers' mental and physical health. (Supplied: Bassina Farbenblum)

"We've seen for a long time that migrant workers are subjected to really appalling accommodation," she said.

"It's terrific to see that the Victorian Labour Hire Authority is now ramping up.

"The proof will be how well it is enforced. Hopefully we will see really strict enforcement."

Ms Farbenblum said living in unhygienic and overcrowded accommodation was "incredibly demeaning".

"We've heard from many migrant workers … the ability to sleep and function is diminished, there's issues with privacy and especially for women there are real safety issues.

"I had one migrant worker describe [their accommodation] as 'not fit for an animal'," she said.

"I'd hope that other states like New South Wales will follow and that we will start to see a real shift in the impunity of labour higher providers that don't provide habitable, decent accommodation to vulnerable migrants."

Industry backs new conditions

Victorian Farmers Federation horticulture president Michael Crisera said the change was a good step for the industry.

"We're definitely supportive of improving conditions for our workers," he said.

"Any industries with labour hire involved definitely need some more compliance."

Mr Crisera said there needed to be education for labour hire providers about what the standards were, as well as education for workers.

"Everybody needs to play a part in making sure that it's a win-win for the staff and also for the farmer," he said.

Accommodation standards already existed but sat with other bodies, such as local councils and Consumer Affairs Victoria.

The standards are now a part of some labour hire licence conditions, which allows the Labour Hire Authority to take action against businesses that do not comply.

The conditions are being applied to new labour hire licences in the horticulture, meat and poultry processing, commercial cleaning, and security industries and will be rolled out to existing licence holders in those sectors in coming months.

title: 'Terrifying' moment Sydney couple's home fell 'to bits' in Colombia quake
text:
After moving to the Colombian city of Cali just over a year ago, Sydney couple Ana Maria Chaves and Christian Bitancurt had settled into life in the country's salsa capital.

"You have to learn how to dance if you live here, you have to learn to salsa otherwise you won't fit in here," Mr Bitancurt said.

However, their lives were uprooted when a magnitude-7.4 earthquake hit the country's west last Monday.

"We all just dived under the table, and our dog is quite big, he's a German shepherd, we couldn't fit him under the table," Ms Chaves, who previously called Daceyville in Sydney's east home, said.

Mr Bitancurt and Ms Chaves took cover under a table when the earthquake hit their hometown of Cali. (Supplied)

While taking shelter under their dining table with Ms Chaves's elderly mother, a wall in their third-floor apartment fell on top of them.

"The sound of the building where you live just falling to bits is terrifying," Mr Bitancurt said.

After the shaking stopped, they made their way outside to find their new city in ruins.

"What we saw is just a whole bunch of people crying, desperate, looking shocked, not knowing what to do because there's no communication," Mr Bitancurt said.

A magnitude-7.4 earthquake hit Colombia on August 10. (Supplied)

Their high-rise apartment has now been deemed too unstable to live in, the couple only returning briefly to grab essentials like clothes and medications.

"We have to start from scratch, we had already set up our home here and we're looking at having to start from zero," Ms Chaves said.

They have moved in temporarily with Ms Chaves's step-mother, grateful to have "a bed to sleep in" while they work out their next steps.

The couple's apartment is now considered too unstable to live in. (Supplied)

Local fundraising efforts

On the other side of the world, members of Sydney's Colombian community shared traditional food and music in support of those back home.

There are nearly 11,000 people who were born in Colombia living in Sydney.

Gathering at a Colombian restaurant in Ashfield in Sydney's inner west, many attendees had family and friends impacted by the earthquake.

The fundraising event at Ashfield was organised by Ms Valencia. (ABC News: Abubakr Sajid)

Organiser Daniela Valencia said her sister had lost all her possessions.

"We are very far away and we decided to do at least something to help all families," Ms Valencia said.

Funds raised by the event, which included a raffle, DJ and performances, were being donated to the Red Cross.

"We need a lot of help, that's why we are calling all communities, all Latin community and even the Aussie community to help us," she said.

Money from the fundraiser will go to the Red Cross. (ABC News: Abubakr Sajid)

Daniel Sarmiento came to enjoy a fried fish, coconut rice and plantain lunch.

"We cannot go to support our family our friends, so we try to do something like come here to buy some lunch," Mr Sarmiento said.

"We are sad, but we are together, we are stronger if we are together."

Close to 11,000 people born in Colombia live in Sydney. (ABC News: Abubakr Sajid)

'We need to just survive and get through this'

As recovery efforts continued in Cali, walking around the streets was still dangerous.

"You do have to be careful as to not walk too close to some of these buildings, because they are very, very damaged," Ms Chaves said.

Taking things "one day at a time," the couple are unsure where they will live or what the future will hold.

"We have no answers right now, we need to just survive and get through this."

Rescue efforts in Cali are ongoing. (Supplied)

But one thing Ms Chaves and Mr Bitancurt have been able to find comfort in is people pulling together as a community.

When they went to volunteer at a nearby collapsed building, they were turned away.

"There were so many people that the police that were around the barricade said 'Guys go home, because we have too many volunteers'," Ms Chaves said.

"There's been such an overwhelming response of people wanting to help, it's just been beautiful to see that."

title: Bigger, heavier electric trucks driving the streets at all hours – the plan to revolutionise our roads
text:

PoliticsFederalRoads Bigger, heavier electric trucks driving the streets at all hours – the plan to revolutionise our roads Shane Wright August 17, 2026 — 11:46am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Larger and heavier trucks would be allowed to deliver around-the-clock under a plan proponents claim would save the industry, businesses and consumers billions of dollars every year. In its final report into the heavy transport sector, the Productivity Commission found that there has been almost no improvement for almost two decades in the ability of trucks to carry loads and get them to their destinations quickly and cheaply – reforms that could draw the ire of residents and local councils. Tesla’s Semi has screens on either side of the steering wheel that provide a view of the traffic around the vehicle The New York Times It found the recent surge in diesel prices caused by the US war against Iran had highlighted the importance of the trucking sector moving towards electric vehicles that would both reduce operational costs, cut noise and enable the more efficient delivery of goods around the country while also reducing greenhouse gas emissions. Australia’s productivity levels have been stagnant this decade, contributing to a drop in living standards. The government announced a $10 billion productivity package in the budget, which included a range of measures including cuts to red tape aimed at small businesses, the axing of 497 nuisance tariffs and plans to reduce heavy transport costs.

Advertisement

The Productivity Commission report said the heavy vehicle transport sector accounted for 5 per cent of GDP, directly employed 273,000 people and was pivotal to the day-to-day functioning of the economy. Related Article Electric vehicles Tesla’s newest electric vehicle could give it a much-needed spark Despite its importance to the economy, the commission found that after a steady increase in productivity from the 1970s to the mid-2000s, it had effectively flatlined for the past 20 years. According to the commission, advances in truck technology with the advent of electric prime movers meant limits on how much trucks can carry should be increased by several tonnes in a move that would boost the economy by up to $2.7 billion. The commission found that while heavier loads would do more damage to roads, the financial benefits would outweigh repair costs.

Advertisement

Further benefits worth up to $2 billion could be generated by overhauling the paperwork required for trucks to use particular roads and the training system for drivers. The advent of quiet electric trucks should also be used to either end or sharply reduce the curfews enforced by states and local councils on delivery services. In some local government areas, for instance, internal combustion engine trucks are prevented from delivering goods to supermarkets between 10pm and 6am. Rolling out specialist electric chargers for trucks would help Australia upgrade its vehicle fleet, the commission argued, saying this was key to boosting productivity and reducing reliance on diesel. “The largest potential productivity benefits will arise from reforms that increase access to Australia’s road network for high productivity vehicles. “The recent fuel supply disruption has only strengthened the case for reform to unlock higher productivity and lower emissions vehicles.”

Advertisement

The commission noted that while many nations were heavily investing in electric trucks, Australian transport companies were sticking with internal combustion vehicles. Related Article GST A $60b GST fiasco: State vs state argument erupts between WA and ‘east coast whingers’ Across China, more than a quarter of all new trucks are electric. Three years ago, they accounted for seven per cent. There has also been large interest in the US, with Tesla starting mass production of its electric Semi earlier this year. Companies such as Walmart and Pepsico have bought hundreds of the vehicles, which have a range of up to 500 miles (800 kilometres), report higher safety levels and can maintain speed in mountainous areas much better than their internal combustion engine counterparts.

Advertisement

NationalNSWCity life Peter paid $2.1m for a Sydney substation. A council error has cost him $800,000 David Barwell August 17, 2026 — 11:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

An inner west property owner says an error by his local council has left him facing financial ruin after he purchased a historic Newtown electricity substation that was incorrectly listed in official planning documents as free from heritage constraints. When Peter Mistrevski bought the decommissioned 1931 brick substation on Probert Street in July last year, he believed he had found a rare foothold in Sydney’s property market and an opportunity to convert the site into two homes, living in one and selling the other. Peter Mistrevski, pictured outside the substation in Newtown. Sam Mooy Before committing to the purchase, Mistrevski obtained a planning certificate from Inner West Council in March 2025 stating the property was not a heritage item, was not within a heritage conservation area and could be redeveloped under the complying development pathway, avoiding the need for a full development application. He said he relied on that certificate, seen by this publication, having it reviewed by his lawyer, architect and town planner as part of his pre-purchase due diligence. He bought the property for $2.1 million at auction.

Advertisement

“I got all the right advice. The planning certificate showed it wasn’t heritage, my town planner and architect looked at it, so I was full steam ahead,” Mistrevski said. But shortly after dotted lines on contracts were signed, a second planning certificate issued by the council in October 2025 identified the property as a heritage-listed building located within a heritage conservation area that could not be redesigned or developed under the same complying development pathway Mistrevski had planned to pursue. Mistrevski bought the property in July last year. Sam Mooy The listing effectively halted the proposed development and plunged the site into planning and legal uncertainty which Mistrevski says is now costing him $12,000 a month in holding fees, while an independent valuation has put the property at $1.3 million – $800,000 below what he paid. “The council made a massive mistake on an official document which I relied on to buy the property,” he said.

Advertisement

“I’m now unable to touch the property, modify it, I can’t live in it. It’s sending me bankrupt and [every] dollar I make is going towards the mortgage to keep the bank from repossessing it. “I tried to make lemonade and I’ve been left with a lemon.” The interior of the building. Sam Mooy The dispute is particularly fraught due to the former utility building’s history, with records showing it was constructed in 1931 during a period when substations were built across Sydney to power homes and businesses as the city grew. In recent years, decommissioned substations have attracted renewed interest from buyers seeking redevelopment opportunities in land-constrained parts of the city, with some small sites selling for more than $2 million despite the planning complexities they can present.

Advertisement

Mistrevski said the heritage listing forced him to redesign his original proposal. A development application lodged at the council in March now proposes retaining the existing substation and constructing a two-storey home behind it. But he said heritage restrictions had significantly increased costs, with planning and development expenses rising from about $50,000 to $150,000 because of the need to engage specialist heritage consultants on the revised plans. A concept image of Mistrevski’s current development plan for the site which proposes a two-storey home at the rear of the property. The application has also undergone multiple revisions in response to council concerns over the scale and bulk of the proposals and its impact on the character of the substation. More than a year after the purchase, the council has yet to determine the application. The dispute has escalated into a compensation claim against the council, with Mistrevski’s lawyers alleging the incorrect planning certificate caused substantial financial losses, including the reduction in the property’s value and lost development opportunities.

Advertisement

An Inner West Council spokesman said it could not comment on the planning certificate because the matter was subject to legal proceedings. “The development application is currently being assessed and all normal processes are being followed,” he said. Mistrevski outside the substation which dates back to 1931. Sam Mooy “More broadly, council is committed to balancing housing needs with protecting heritage.” Mistrevski said the 12-month ordeal had exposed the risks buyers face when relying on official planning information and argued purchasers should be able to have confidence in the accuracy of council-issued documents before committing to major property purchases.

Advertisement

“Buying a home is the biggest financial commitment most people will ever make and I feel like I’m being punished for a mistake I didn’t make,” he said. “All I’m asking for is a fair go.” Be the first to know when major news happens. The words were a sign that Solomon believes that whoever wins the coaching gig will need to reclaim the faith of a frustrated group of supporters, who have not seen a win at the MCG since the middle of last season. In an infamous 1996 interview with 60 Minutes, Hanson responded "I don't like it" while offering her thoughts on the annual LGBTQI+ festival.

"I don't like it because it's promoting something ... that is not natural," she said at the time.

Her "I don't like it" comment was co-opted by musician Simon Hunt, also known as drag queen Pauline Pantsdown, in 1998, and remixed into a parody dance song that made the Triple J Hottest 100 that year.
