Musician Simon Hunt, also known as drag queen Pauline Pantsdown, had a hit dance song parodying Pauline Hanson. Source: AAP / Danny Casey

Three decades later, Hanson said she acknowledged the economic benefit of the pride parade, adding that it was "acceptable" Australia had legalised gay marriage.

"I still don't like the gay Mardi Gras, but that's my opinion," she told News24 on Sunday.

"Have I ever been to one? No. Do I intend to go? No, I don't.

"I think your own personal sexuality should be kept ... behind closed doors. It's no one's business to do it out there with the gay Mardi Gras anywhere.

"I know it brings a lot of tourists to the country. I know it brings a lot of money. I know all this, but that’s my personal opinion. But anyway, good luck to them that they want to do that."

Her comments follow revelations One Nation's candidate for Western Australia's upper house at the 2025 election, Parminder Singh, made several anti-gay comments in a video on social media.

Singh, who was third on One Nation's upper house ticket at the state election, has since been removed from the party's website.

During the week, One Nation MP Barnaby distanced the party from its former candidate's views, describing it as "one of the gayest parties in Australia".

Hanson also rejected Singh's comments, saying she never heard similar views from him when he was a candidate.

"That's his personal thoughts and not my thoughts whatsoever," she said.

Hanson defends inability to name world leaders

The firebrand politician also defended her inability to name the leaders of crucial allies and regional powers when questioned about her foreign policy credentials as a would-be prime minister.

In an earlier interview with News24, the One Nation leader said diplomacy with Australia's neighbours would pose "no problem", despite her notoriously using her maiden speech in 1996 to declare the nation was "in danger of being swamped by Asians".

Asked if she could name the president of Indonesia or the prime minister of Japan, two major regional powers and key Australian trading partners, Hanson said she couldn't.

On Sunday, she said she would learn the names when it was necessary.

"I still haven't looked up who the prime minister of Indonesia is because I don't need to know ... I'm not the foreign minister, I'm not the prime minister," Hanson said.

The One Nation leader also reiterated her party's position that Australia's net migration target should be 130,000 a year — a significant cut on current levels.

She suggested the reduction could come at the expense of international students, a major source of income for universities, describing the intake system as a "farce" and a "scam" that provides a backdoor into the nation.

But she was adamant any cut to migration should not alter backpacker levels.

"We cannot stop those people coming in; if they did, the farmers would go under," Hanson said.

None of the major parties have outlined which visa categories should be cut to meet their reduced migration targets.

title: Fiji, Israel and the Lost Tribe at the ends of the Earth
text:
This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.

Long ago, the story goes, a great double-hulled canoe called the Kaunitoni came from the west, carrying the first ancestral chiefs of the iTaukei (indigenous Fijians). At its head, in one version of the tradition, stood their leader, Lutunasobasoba.

The voyagers had come a seemingly impossible distance: from Thebes in ancient Egypt — earlier still, some say, from a place farther west, via Israel — down the Nile to Lake Tanganyika, across the Indian Ocean, and finally to Vuda, on the western coast of Viti Levu, Fiji's largest island.

Somewhere in that crossing, a sacred box went over the side.

In some tellings, it carried the written record of the people's laws and genealogies — lost, like the canoe's other cargo, somewhere in the churning sea.

For most of the past century, this has been one of the best-known versions of Fiji's national origin story. The mission schools taught it; so did the primary schools. Radio carried it further still, until it became part of the way generations of Fijians understood their ancestry.

Only, much of it was invented in the 1890s — set down for the first time in a newspaper.

The colonial government's Fijian-language paper, Na Mata, ran a competition at the time, inviting readers across the archipelago to send in the definitive account of where the Fijian people had come from, with the best to be printed.

The winning entry ran over 17 instalments, centring on a forgotten tribe. Within a few decades it had acquired the weight of history.

The shape of the belief

The story of the Kaunitoni is only one part of the overall narrative.

Behind the claimed migration sits a larger conviction, still widely held in some iTaukei communities and church groups: that Fijians descend from a Lost Tribe of Israel — one of 10 the Hebrew Bible describes as carried into exile and never heard from again.

The belief has no support in mainstream science or archaeology. Yet it has helped foster a distinctive affinity with Israel.

An artistic depiction of the Kaunitoni, the double-hulled canoe at the centre of Fiji's best-known origin story. Source: SBS News / Jacob Chantarat

The particulars shift from place to place. On Mana Island, in the Yasawa group off western Viti Levu, the Ark of the Covenant — the gold-covered chest that, in the Book of Exodus, held the Ten Commandments — is said to lie buried.

In a village in Ba, in Viti Levu's north-west, an elder once pointed to a rock and told Reverend Marika Baleidelabaci, a Fijian historian and Methodist minister, that Jesus had been born exactly there.

In the Navosa highlands, markings cut into a cave wall are read by some as ancient Hebrew — an interpretation, Baleidelabaci says, that came back with Fijian soldiers who had served in the Middle East and recognised the shapes.

"Nobody knows the origin of that writing," he tells SBS News of the unverified petroglyphs.

They assumed that it must be Jewish.

Believers offer corroborations: circumcision is said to predate the missionaries; Fiji is read as an acronym for Father of Israel, Jewish Island; the tanoa, the carved bowl in which the yaqona (kava) drink is served, is claimed to take its name from a phrase meaning "built by Noah".

Anthropologist Lynda Newland, writing in 2015, described the idea that certain iTaukei clans descend from a Lost Tribe as "very strong among some contemporary clans and church groups". Her research traces the belief through the intersection of Christianity, Fijian traditions and ideas about ancestry.

Edwin Jones, who spent a year in the highland district of Nabobuco, found it had "gained currency" among Methodists of the interior — held there alongside their own belief that the ancestors emerged from the Nakauvadra hills.

Christians make up around two-thirds of Fiji's population, and more than half of them are Methodist — a church whose preaching draws heavily on the Hebrew Bible. One former president of the Methodist Church in Fiji estimated 95 per cent of sermons were taken from the Old Testament.

A map of the Kaunitoni voyage as the story describes it — out of Egypt, along the African lakes, and east across two oceans. Source: SBS News

Beyond Fiji, iterations of the same idea have taken root across Melanesia.

In western Papua New Guinea, the Gogodala have been reported to perform Hebrew prayers and incorporate biblical-Israelite ideas into religious practice.

On Malaita, the most populous island of Solomon Islands, the late Anglican visionary George Umai taught that his ancestors had fled Jerusalem in the first century and buried the Ark in the bush at Kwara'ae. There, Israeli flags still hang in village churches, a visible expression of the close ties some Pacific communities have developed with their perceived motherland.

Why the Pacific votes with Israel

In the past three years, that connection has become visible in foreign policy.

When the United Nations General Assembly voted in October 2023 on a ceasefire in Gaza, 14 countries opposed it. Six were Pacific Island states: Fiji, Papua New Guinea, Nauru, Tonga, the Marshall Islands and Micronesia — among the smallest nations on Earth and together accounting for nearly half of the votes against the resolution.

The resolution called for an immediate humanitarian truce but did not explicitly mention Hamas' October 7 attacks, an omission several countries, including Fiji, cited in explaining their objections.

Fijian Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka (left) and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu at the opening of Fiji's embassy in Jerusalem on 17 September 2025. Credit: Fiji Ministry of Foreign Affairs

Fiji's position is also shaped by domestic politics.

The country's Jerusalem embassy, opened in September 2025, has its roots in a 2022 election that left parliament deadlocked and gave the nationalist Social Democratic Liberal Party (SODELPA) the balance of power in coalition talks. SODELPA leader Viliame Gavoka had campaigned on a promise to establish an embassy in Jerusalem. Sitiveni Rabuka, who became prime minister after forming a coalition with SODELPA, agreed to the proposal, with Gavoka becoming his deputy.

Meanwhile, Papua New Guinea opened an embassy in Jerusalem in 2023, with Israel underwriting the running costs. Samoa announced its own in early 2026, and in July, Nauru became the latest Pacific country to announce plans to do so.

Jerusalem's status remains sensitive and complex, as it is contested between the Israelis and the Palestinians. The Israelis claim it as their capital, and Israel's parliament, the Knesset, is based there.

For Palestinians, it is their historical, religious and cultural capital, home to the Al-Aqsa Mosque, considered the third holiest site in Islam, and the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, the most sacred site in Christianity.

Israel has occupied East Jerusalem since 1967, annexing the area in 1980.

Fiji has contributed troops to UN peacekeeping missions in the Middle East since the late 1970s, and remains among the largest per-capita contributors of peacekeepers in the world. Source: AP / Hanin Network Website

Israel has been expanding in the other direction too, opening an embassy in Fiji's capital Suva in June — a regional hub intended to deepen ties with Fiji and across the wider Pacific.

But the political relationship has another layer. Behind the growth in political ties is decades of work by the International Christian Embassy Jerusalem (ICEJ), an evangelical Christian Zionist group founded in 1980 that has campaigned in Pacific churches for years, and whose Fiji branch its leadership has praised as a model for pro-Israel Christians worldwide. SBS News contacted the ICEJ for comment but received no response.

The attachment to the holy land is expressed in other ways too. Relative to its population, Fiji has sent more soldiers to UN peacekeeping missions than any other country in the world — many of which have been carried out in the Middle East. Believers of the Kaunitoni origin story also make regular pilgrimages to Israel.

In early October 2023, Fijian pilgrims stood in the Negev desert near the Gaza border, planting oak seedlings in the dry yellow dirt and watering them from a bottle of Fiji Water. They had travelled for Sukkot, the Jewish harvest festival, believing themselves to be returning to ancestral land.

Two days later, Hamas militants led the coordinated October 7 attack into southern Israel, leading to Israel's invasion of the now-devastated enclave.

Brian Dunn is a church historian who emigrated to Fiji from Canada in mid-2023 and is now the head of history at Pasifika Communities University. He says many of those who have returned from peacekeeping tours describe them in unexpectedly personal terms.

"Some even looked at their tour of duty as a pilgrimage," Dunn tells SBS News.

"I hadn't really noticed until October 7 just how fully and completely it seems like the vast majority of Fijians were putting their support behind the nation state of Israel."

How Fiji's Kaunitoni origin story came to be

To understand how a newspaper entry came to shape Fiji's origin story, we have to go back 40 years before it ran — to two Wesleyan missionaries, William Cross and David Cargill, who landed in 1835 on the island of Lakeba, in Fiji's far east, carrying the Old Testament.

Fijians heard of a people chosen by God and organised into 12 tribes, each descended from a common ancestor — and Fijian society was built the same way, in clans tracing descent from a founding ancestor, each with its own plant or animal totem.

"They tried to assimilate themselves with the Jews," Baleidelabaci says.

The idea took written form in the mission schools. In a 2003 doctoral thesis, the Fijian Methodist minister Tevita Baleiwaqa traces it to the seminary that trained Fiji's first indigenous ministers, where students schooled in the Old Testament began reading their own past through biblical narratives.

Anthropologist Lynda Newland finds no trace of the Lost Tribes idea in Fiji before Cession in 1874 — when sovereignty was handed to Britain — and argues it surfaces a decade or two later — once Christianity and Victorian science had supplied "a grammar for it".

The Israeli and Fijian flags fly outside Suva's Grand Pacific Hotel in late October 2025, weeks after Fiji opened its embassy in Jerusalem. Source: SBS, Supplied

That science was diffusionism: the belief that complex cultural practices could not have developed independently in different places, and must instead have spread from a common ancient source, often located somewhere in the biblical world.

Its method was wordplay. The missionary Jesse Carey, working under the amateur anthropologist Lorimer Fison, gathered resemblances between Fijian and African place names — among them a Vunda near Lake Tanganyika as well as the Vunda in Fiji — and concluded Fijians had come from Africa, and before that from Egypt.

"He homologised these names, though they have no relation whatsoever," Dunn says.

The colonial administration had its own reason to want a single origin story. Fiji had never been one country, but a patchwork of chiefdoms with no paramount ruler — and Britain preferred to govern indirectly, through an existing hierarchy.

A shared ancestry was easier for colonial administrators to govern than a society of hundreds of clans.

READ MORE Former Fiji military commander Sitiveni Rabuka rules out China security pact if he wins government

Which brings the story back to the newspaper. In 1892 the editor of Na Mata announced a competition to select a definitive version of the people's legendary history. No criteria for judging were ever published.

The winning entry ran in seventeen monthly instalments, and its author signed himself Denicagilaba — or Hurricane Clouds.

Three years later Basil Thomson, a colonial official who would go on to chair the Native Lands Commission — the body that decided which clan owned what — translated the story and published it in London.

The identity behind the pseudonym went unrecorded for 70 years. When the historian Peter France established it, on Thomson's authority, Hurricane Clouds turned out to be Ilai Motonococoka — Thomson's own clerk.

"It was like fan fiction," Dunn says.

The ultimate agenda was to bring the land resources under control.

That interpretation is contested, but the story was produced at a time when the colonial government was formalising systems of land ownership and political authority.

Then the empire added a layer. Fiji was expected to pay for itself, and sugar was the crop to do it — but iTaukei land could not be sold, and iTaukei labour could not be easily commandeered for the plantations. So, Britain shipped in workers instead: more than 60,000 Indian indentured labourers arrived between 1879 and 1916, under contracts known as girmit.

To explain two peoples in one colony, missionaries turned to the story of twin brothers Jacob and Esau from the book of Genesis, casting Indo-Fijians as the younger brother Jacob and the iTaukei as Esau the hunter. In the story, the brothers share a lifelong rivalry that culminates in Jacob deceiving his father to gain a blessing intended for his older brother. Missionaries leant on the tale to share a hidden message: the older shall serve the younger.

The 1987 Fiji coups and the politics of identity

In April 1987, an election ended 17 years of rule by the iTaukei-led Alliance Party.

The winning coalition drew its support largely from Indo-Fijians, who by then made up roughly half the population; its prime minister, Timoci Bavadra, was an iTaukei commoner, but most of his cabinet was not.

Within a month, Lieutenant Colonel Sitiveni Rabuka — a Methodist lay preacher — walked into parliament with 10 masked soldiers and removed the government at gunpoint. When a negotiated settlement threatened to restore it in September, he seized power a second time and declared Fiji a republic.

Inside the Methodist Church, the country's largest denomination, a parallel struggle over the church's direction was under way.

For two decades its presidents had been moderates who preached ecumenism (unity among Christian denominations) and multiracialism; the church had elected an Indo-Fijian president as recently as 1977. Manasa Lasaro, its general secretary, moved against that tradition.

Baleidelabaci, who was in Fiji during those years, remembers the language exactly.

"He said the coup was the will of God to free the Fijians, the chosen people, from bondage and from heathen races," he recalls.

"That refers to the Indians."

Lasaro declared Fiji a holy land and its people a holy people, who demanded holy government for all. From the pulpit, Rabuka's soldiers became Joshua, the general who seized Canaan, and the ministers Moses, who brought the people out of bondage.

"The Fijians at that time were only fighting for the rights of the iTaukei," Baleidelabaci says.

"The dominance of iTaukei in Fiji."

Underneath the scripture was a narrative the empire had helped build: one assembled to make Fiji legible to its administrators that had, a century later, been taken up by a nationalist movement — and turned against a population the same empire had brought to the colony.

The Fijian histories left out of the archive

When Dunn repeated the Kaunitoni story to elders in the highland village of Rewasau, deep in the interior and far from the coastal centres where the mission first took hold, they brushed it aside.

"That's not our story," they told him.

We didn't come from anywhere. We've always been here.

Archaeological evidence points to human settlement around 3,000 years ago, associated with the Lapita people, whose distinctive pottery has been found across the Pacific — a very different account from the Kaunitoni story of migration from ancient Egypt.

Baleidelabaci, a Methodist minister himself, is collecting what the archive left out — accounts that survived in the far-flung villages, and nowhere else.

"When they arrived, they said that our stories of our origin were regarded as myths and legends," he says.

"There's a lot of things in my church that need to be reinvestigated. What we are doing now is still new to us."

For Dunn, the correction has to come from the same place the stories do.

"The voice of the communities has really unsettled the text. Most of what actually happened never got written," he says.

Just a tiny sliver made it into the archive — and the very act of writing it into an archive is a power move.

title: 'Won't be the case forever': Australia's housing market is testing a popular assumption
text:
In brief Investors appear to be pulling back but it may be an early reaction to the tax reforms announced in May.

A retreat of investors doesn't mean first-home buyers will fill the gap.

Investors are shying away from the housing market — but experts say it might not be the win the government says it is.

New Australian Bureau of Statistics data on loans show investors have pulled back sharply from the housing market in the June quarter.

Declines in investor loans was the highest since September 2022.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers said on Friday the lending figures were an "encouraging sign" that Labor's changes to negative gearing and the capital gains discount were working as intended and the market was "shifting in favour of first-home buyers" — even before the changes have officially taken effect.

But experts said the retreat hasn't necessarily translated into the wave of first-home buyers the federal government's property tax changes were designed to generate.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

'Not surprising' but not the whole picture

The number of investor loans fell 8.6 per cent in the June quarter, while first-home buyer loans fell a comparatively lower 2.9 per cent, according to ABS data released on Friday.

Independent property researcher Cameron Kusher said ABS' latest lending data was not surprising and reflected a typical knee-jerk reaction to policy changes.

“Across both the number and the value, the biggest falls in lending over the quarter were for investors, which is not really a surprise when you consider the tax changes that have happened,” he said.

Both investors and owner-occupiers have shied off the housing market — but investors saw a much larger dip. Source: SBS News

The pullback lines up with what major banks have been reporting in their own lending figures, with CBA and NAB both reporting a 15 per cent drop in mortgage applications last quarter, while Westpac saw a 20 per cent drop.

The tax changes were announced in the May budget but aren't set to formally take effect until 1 July 2027. So, this quarter's fall was a reaction to the announcement itself, not the policy in action.

Kusher expects a bigger fall in investor lending in the future.

"We may actually see a larger fall when we get to the next quarter, when we see the full impact of a whole quarter of these changes," he said.

Both Kusher and Real Estate Group's economist Luc Redman say investors have not retreated entirely, rather they have changed strategy.

They are still keen on residential property but the type of property they’re chasing has shifted. They are now eyeing properties that have strong rental growth, or yield.

"Early evidence post-budget suggests that investors are enquiring more towards units that tend to have a higher yield and a lower entry point … compared to prior, when investors would be looking at houses that have stronger prospects of capital growth," Redman told SBS News.

Two places, Tasmania and the ACT, didn't see drops in investor interest — which Kusher said could be a sign they're moving toward properties with good rental returns relative to purchase price.

All states saw drops in investor lending except for Tasmania and ACT — perhaps reflecting a desire for properties with strong rental returns. Source: SBS News

"I think the fall in new investment will potentially have a flow-on effect to the rental market where rental supply will tighten and landlords will have more scope to put up rents," Kusher said, though he noted there wasn't evidence of that happening "just yet".

Both experts hesitate to call this a permanent retreat for investors.

"It is likely that this won't be the case forever," Redman said.

"Once yields return to more attractive levels, we would expect investors to return to the market at a new equilibrium," he said.

"In the short term in particular, there will probably be a higher proportion of owner-occupier purchases in the market until we see yields rebalance and investor sentiment return ... [separately] the structural undersupply of dwellings means prices will continue to increase over the long run, albeit more modestly than recent price growth."

Kusher says at least two to three quarters of data will be needed before drawing any meaningful conclusions, meaning the next quarterly release will be a better indication of investor behaviour as it will be the first to reflect a full three months under the new environment.

A win for first-home buyers?

The policy case for the tax changes rested on the idea that pushing investors out would clear space for first-home buyers.

But the numbers haven't quite shown that yet, Kusher says, adding that two things may be happening.

First-home buyers do not directly replace all the investors who have retreated — first-home buyers do not entirely fill the gap as they are a smaller group of buyers than investors. Secondly, first-home buyers, like investors, are also in a “wait and see” mode.

"There's an assumption that if you don't have an investor, you have a first-home buyer. That's not always the case. Not everyone that's currently renting is in a position to buy a home,” Kusher said.

Investors make up about 40 per cent of the residential market, but first-home buyers have never been that large a group, he added.

"So, if you're discouraging investors and trying to encourage first-time buyers, you're probably going to struggle to see an uplift in first-home buyer lending offset the weakness in investor lending — and that's certainly what we've seen,” Kusher said.

He notes that some first-home buyers may be falling into a "trap" of trying to time a falling market but warns “picking the bottom of the market” is incredibly difficult.

"I think what these [tax] changes have done more than anything else is just damaged sentiment around the housing market," he said.

title: Beautiful, remote and running on diesel: The Daintree's power struggle
text:
This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.

In her backyard, Tamara Scenna takes a deep breath beneath the towering canopy of the Daintree Rainforest in Far North Queensland.

Streams of light filter through layers of ferns and fan palms as she pauses beside a running stream.

Birds sing in an off-beat chorus, providing a tranquil soundtrack to one of the oldest rainforests.

It's the perfect setting for forest bathing — a Japanese practice of immersing oneself in nature.

"I think it's about seeing the forest differently and being able to almost be given permission to slow down and stop and just be," Scenna tells SBS News.

"It took a while to slow down and really have a city adrenaline stop, but after a couple of months we sort of went, 'actually we don't want to go to the city anymore'.

"We'd rather spend the time out in nature."

But behind the tranquillity lies a challenge shared by many of the Daintree's roughly 700 residents. Living beyond the electricity grid means finding ways to balance life in this remote rainforest with the realities of modern living.

Living beyond the grid

In 2021, Scenna and her family swapped life in Sydney for the quiet of the UNESCO World Heritage-listed Daintree Rainforest.

Hoping to escape the pace of city life, her family spent a year travelling around Australia before deciding they were ready for a change.

In 2021, Tamara Scenna left her public sector career in Sydney for a quieter life in the Daintree Rainforest. Source: SBS News / Jesmine Cheong

The journey led the couple to settle in the rainforest, with Scenna leaving her public sector job to run a caravan park and restaurant with her husband , Bruno.

But the dream of living among the ancient trees comes with practical challenges. Like many residents in the region, the couple must find their own solutions for powering their home and business.

While the Scennas have a hybrid energy system that includes solar, relying on diesel generators remains a necessity.

They paid about $300,000 for the solar that powers around a third of their business.

Bruno says installing enough solar panels to power their entire operation would be expensive and require clearing more rainforest for additional infrastructure.

We are basically burning diesel rather than having a renewable microgrid; it makes no sense whatsoever.

"From an environmental perspective, why would you do that when you can have renewable energy? I fundamentally don't understand," he tells SBS News.

The cost of living off-grid

Growing uncertainty around fuel costs, including volatility linked to global events, has renewed calls from residents for a renewable energy solution in the Daintree.

In 2022, a solar-based microgrid project received a funding commitment of $18.75 million from the then Coalition federal government, with funding to start in 2025.

The proposed project included an 8-megawatt solar farm, a 20-megawatt-hour battery storage system, and a 1-megawatt hydrogen plant. However, the current Labor government withdrew the funding in 2024, leaving the project without the grant needed to proceed.

In the lush landscape of Cape Tribulation, nestled among rolling mountains and dense forest, Lawrence Mason runs a café and fruit orchard in Douglas Shire.

To keep his business running, he burns about 700 litres of diesel every week — a cost that has grown as fuel prices surpassed $3 a litre earlier this year.

Lawrence Mason runs a café and a fruit orchard in Cape Tribulation, a headland and coastal locality in Douglas Shire in northern Queensland. Source: SBS News / Jesmine Cheong

For Mason, the rising cost of generating electricity has affected the future of his business in the rainforest.

I don't want to leave this place, it's my home.

"But there does come a time in everyone's life and I think it doesn't matter where you live, where you have to make practical decisions for your future," he tells SBS News.

His grandparents moved to the region almost a century ago and lived off the land, working as timber cutters and later cattle farmers.

Mason has spent his whole life connected to the tourism industry in the region.

"They're [tourists] coming to what is [one of] the oldest rainforest[s] in the world, a very beautiful place, and most of them are horrified to learn that we have a government with so little imagination, we're still [using] diesel generators for power."

Ageing off-grid

Confronted with the decision to potentially leave the rainforest, many ageing in the Daintree face a difficult reality.

Resident Chris Reinke, who has lived alone for the last decade, shares similar concerns about whether she can remain in the rainforest long-term.

Chris Reinke has lived in the Daintree since 1983, but says ageing there is becoming harder without mains power. Source: SBS News / Jesmine Cheong

The 71-year-old moved to the region with her late husband in 1983, but says spending her later years there is becoming increasingly difficult without access to mains power.

At the end of the day, I'm going to have to move out as I get older because I'm trying to lift jerry cans for generators.

"If I had mains power or a microgrid, you'd have to carry me out in a box because I wouldn't be leaving until then, because I wouldn't have to worry about generators," Reinke tells SBS News.

Sitting on her veranda tucked between towering canopy trees, Reinke is reminded of the natural beauty that drew her to the Daintree decades ago.

"As soon as I crossed that ferry, it was like I fell in love," she says.

"I just knew this is where I should be, it was just beautiful."

For Betty Hinton, the Daintree has been home for almost five decades — a place where she built a life, an art practice and a small business.

Betty Hinton moved to the rainforest with her late husband nearly 50 years ago, drawn to its picturesque landscapes. Source: SBS News / Jesmine Cheong

The 91-year-old artist moved to the rainforest with her late husband, drawn to its diverse plant life and picturesque landscapes.

"For some people, it would have been difficult, impossible," Hinton tells SBS News.

"But for us, because we just love the area, we were excited about the chance to live here.

"It was a lot of hard work; there was nothing here, we had to build everything."

Today, Hinton runs an ice cream business that relies on costly generators, selling a variety of flavours , including a signature green ice cream inspired by the rainforest.

She still services her own generators, a physically demanding task involving changing filters and carrying heavy oil.

The cost of getting help to maintain the equipment can also be prohibitive in such a remote location.

"When I got the bill, I nearly died, they [tradespeople] charged me $600 to change the oil," she says.

"What do you say? What options do I have?"

It's a lot of work that I don't enjoy, it's a lot of expense that it's very difficult for a small business to maintain.

The debate over a Daintree microgrid

Former federal member for Leichhardt Warren Entsch, who was in parliament for 26 years, spent years of his career campaigning for a microgrid project in the Daintree.

"So many businesses have started and failed because of the cost of generation of power," he tells SBS News.

It is just so grossly unfair.

"You've got an older population here that cannot deal with this."

Former federal member for Leichhardt Warren Entsch has spent years campaigning for a microgrid project in the Daintree Rainforest. Source: SBS News / Jesmine Cheong

While some residents and community leaders see a microgrid as a way to provide more reliable renewable energy, others argue that development in the world-heritage-listed rainforest must be carefully managed.

Former Douglas Shire mayor Mike Berwick says: "Biologically, this is an incredibly valuable place and the priority should be helping people to live with minimal impact."

"And that means don't build a bridge, don't widen the road, don't urbanise the place, don't put grid power in there, but help people to live independently with a life footprint."

When asked if the federal government would reconsider funding for the project, Energy Minister Chris Bowen said the Albanese government was investing in microgrid projects in regional and First Nations communities.

"The Daintree Microgrid Project was given every opportunity to meet requirements they were contractually obligated to meet, but they failed to do so, and the grant funding ceased," he said in an earlier statement.

The company developing the grid, Volt Advisory Group, disputes the government's account, saying Cyclone Jasper in December 2023 caused unprecedented damage to the Douglas Shire road network and prevented heavy construction machinery from reaching the site for many months.

"Despite the disaster's force majeure status being acknowledged and approvals being in place, the project was unable to get the government to extend the grant to allow the project to be built once roads were restored," it said in a statement to SBS News.

First Nations calls for renewable energy

For Eastern Kuku Yalanji people, the conversation about power in the Daintree is connected to culture, Country and the ability to live on ancestral land.

In the remote Aboriginal community of Wujal Wujal, north of the Daintree Rainforest, Kathleen and Francis Walker sing out to their ancestors at a waterfall.

The Eastern Kuku Yalanji Elders are calling on the federal government to reconsider funding a microgrid in the Daintree , saying reliable power could help First Nations people return to Country.

Kathleen and Francis Walker are calling on the federal government to reconsider funding a microgrid in the Daintree. Source: SBS News / Jesmine Cheong

Known as the rainforest people, the Eastern Kuku Yalanji have deep cultural ties to the area, including through cultural sites, Dreamtime stories and totemic animals.

Francis Walker, who is a dialysis patient, believes having reliable power in the Daintree would help her live back on Country.

"If that microgrid did go ahead for me, I'd be happy to be living on my land instead of living in another place where I'm not happy," she tells SBS News.

My wawu [spirit] is here at home.

In 2021, the Daintree National Park was formally handed back to Traditional Owners in a historic agreement that established joint management of the area with the Queensland government.

Jabalbina Aboriginal Corporation, which represents Eastern Kuku Yalanji Traditional Owners, is also advocating for investment in renewable energy infrastructure for the region.

Culture and language manager Trinity Clarke says reliable infrastructure could help more First Nations people live on Country and maintain their connection to culture.

"It's still ongoing today, like families still reconnecting back with who they were, their bubu, where they're from and their family lines, it's still devastating," she tells SBS News.

"If we don't live on Country and speak to Country, we lose that part of ourselves and our mob don't want any more loss."

Kathleen Walker wants to live the rest of her life on the land of her ancestors and continue traditional practices. Source: SBS News / Jesmine Cheong

It's a connection that resonates with Kathleen Walker, who wants the opportunity to live on the land of her ancestors and continue traditional practices.

"Like the trees, you know, when they get old, they die in the rainforest," she tells SBS News.

"Well, bama [people] wants to be like that.

Bama wants to die and have a rest in peace in their homeland.

title: More GPs are asking patients this question. What should you do?
text:
In Brief An estimated 40 per cent of general practitioners use AI scribes in their consultations.

Experts are divided over their benefits and drawbacks, with bigger questions around privacy and regulatory oversight remaining.

Walk into a GP's room these days, and you might be asked something new: "Do you consent to me using an AI transcription tool?"

It's a question that could soon become routine, with AI scribes now used by roughly 40 per cent of Australian GPs, up from 22 per cent in August 2024, according to survey data from the Royal Australian College of General Practitioners (RACGP).

Dr Janice Tan, a spokesperson for RACGP's expert committee, said GPs and clinicians use AI scribes to transcribe conversations with patients, take automated notes, and summarise what was discussed.

"During the consult, they [the AI scribe] listen and produce a draft note afterwards," she told SBS News. "Many also draft referral and specialist letters, care plans, and sometimes a plain-English summary for the patient."

But she's clear that the software documents interactions — it doesn't decide care plans.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"A product that starts suggesting a diagnosis or treatment the clinician didn't state is no longer a scribe, and sits in a different regulatory category," she said.

But another expert said more safeguards are needed to protect patients — and the benefits aren't as clear-cut as they first appear.

The good

For GPs, Tan said the appeal comes down to reduced burnout and more patient-centred care.

"There's less documentation after hours, which is a real driver of burnout and people leaving the profession," she said.

"The doctor is looking at you rather than the keyboard … there's more patient-centred consults, not quicker ones."

"The most underused benefit is the patient-facing summary … [which features] what we discussed, what changed, when to come back. That's valuable for anyone managing something complex, and for carers."

She also said it allows for "better and more consistent records", which are particularly helpful if you don't always see the same GP.

The bad

Andrew Cullen from the University of Melbourne's School of Computing and Information Systems agrees GPs are the clear winners — but is more cautious about what patients get out of it.

"GPs and clinicians love scribes, because they no longer need to take notes — so they can devote more time to their patients," he told SBS News. "However, for patients, the benefit is a lot less clear."

His main concern is 'hallucination' — when AI systems, including scribes, confidently make up facts. He cited a 2025 study which he said found "up to 20 per cent of notes made by AI scribes contained major errors".

"The quality of these notes is hugely important — they're the way doctors keep track of patients long term, and how they share concerns with specialists," he said.

"So if AI gets things wrong, patients can be misdiagnosed, or provided inappropriate care, based upon an AI's mistakes."

Tan said the most common error type is omission — where details are left out — which she puts at roughly three-quarters of all errors.

"They're the hardest to catch because you have to notice something isn't there," she said.

Both experts flag the tools can also struggle with strong accents, speech impediments, or noisy rooms, raising equity questions about who the technology best serves — though Tan notes this is improving with newer models.

The bigger questions

Bigger questions around regulation and privacy still surround the technology, with the two experts split on whether current oversight goes far enough.

Privacy

Concerns around how AI tools handle personal information aren't unique to healthcare — but Cullen argues the stakes are higher here than in most industries.

"We don't know how these notes are being used, we don't know how safely they're being held, and clinicians aren't well equipped to handle these conversations within an appointment," he said.

"Patients really need an empowered regulator, supported by government, to actively look out for their interests, to ensure that their private medical information is treated safely, and that their data is protected."

Tan said retention of audio files varies by product, while draft notes go into the practice's clinical software, where they're covered by the Privacy Act and state health records legislation like any other health record.

"RACGP advises practices to check where data is stored and processed and whether the vendor can reuse it for other purposes," she said. "Asking your practice whether that check was done is fair."

Regulations

Then there's the question of whether an AI scribe constitutes a medical device, which are subject to far stricter regulatory oversight.

While AI scribes are covered by multiple regulatory frameworks, including the Privacy Act and guidance from the Australian Health Practitioner Regulation Agency, oversight from the Therapeutic Goods Administration only applies if a tool crosses into medical device territory.

"A scribe becomes a medical device once it interprets the conversation, including generating a diagnosis or treatment recommendation the clinician didn't state," Tan said. "That's the right line in the sand."

READ MORE I had a high chance of getting cancer, so I turned to AI to save me

Cullen argues that threshold "completely misses the risk that biases and mistakes in an AI's output could affect diagnoses" and said there is a need for further safeguards.

"Treating a scribe as a medical device would require the companies behind these systems to perform much more rigorous testing, and to be far more open about who has access to patient information," he said, adding that other countries have moved to treat AI scribes as medical devices.

But Tan cautions against regulatory overcorrection.

"Make compliant tools hard to use, and clinicians will reach for ungoverned ones on personal devices, which is a worse outcome for patients," she said.

She said that, ultimately, an AI scribe requires clinician oversight — and patient consent.

"Like every tool in medicine, it needs training, oversight, checks, and a clinician who takes responsibility for the output," she said.

"If patients take one thing away: being asked for consent is a good sign, and asking your GP what happens to the recording is a reasonable question."

title: The major citizenship ruling affecting Australians like Ophelia
text:
IN BRIEF An Italian court's ruling could revive claims rejected under the so-called 'minor issue' interpretation of citizenship law.

But new citizenship restrictions mean some applicants still face additional hurdles under Italy's current rules.

When Ophelia Bryant first travelled to Italy in 1986, she says she felt something she could not quite explain.

"It just felt like I came home," she told SBS News.

Her parents had been born in Italy, as had all four of her grandparents. They immigrated to Australia in 1955, where Bryant was born three years later.

Italy has remained a constant in her life, with Bryant returning more than a dozen times to visit relatives and reconnect with her family roots.

But when she began looking into whether she could formally claim Italian citizenship, she discovered her family history came with a legal complication.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Her parents became Australian citizens in 1961, when Bryant was a child, and later formally renounced their Italian citizenship.

Ophelia Bryant's parents were born in Italy, as were all four of her grandparents. Her parents immigrated to Australia in 1955, where she was born three years later. Source: Supplied / (Supplied: Ophelia Bryant)

Under a restrictive interpretation of Italy's citizenship laws, known as the 'minor issue', that could break the line of citizenship transmission.

"I thought the door was closed because of that minor rule," Bryant said.

Now, a landmark decision by Italy's highest court has changed that legal interpretation — and Bryant is "optimistic because that door may finally be open".

A rule that divided Italian citizenship cases

The so-called minor issue arose from conflicting interpretations of Italy's 1912 citizenship law.

One provision established that children born overseas to an Italian citizen could acquire Italian citizenship from birth.

Another was interpreted as meaning that when an Italian parent became a citizen of another country, their minor children could lose their Italian citizenship along with them.

That interpretation gained ground through Italian court decisions from 2023 onwards, leading to the rejection of citizenship-by-descent applications.

But in July, Italy's Supreme Court's United Sections, the court's highest panel for resolving conflicting legal interpretations, ruled that citizenship acquired at birth was not automatically lost when an Italian parent subsequently naturalised in another country.

Brisbane-based Italian lawyer Fabrizio Fiorino, who advises clients on Italian citizenship applications, said the decision effectively restores the previous interpretation of the law.

"It was not a change in a provision, but it was a change in the interpretation of rules," he said.

When Ophelia Bryant first travelled to Italy in 1986, she says she felt something she could not quite explain. Source: Supplied / Ophelia Bryant

He told SBS News the ruling means people who were Italian citizens from birth cannot simply be considered to have lost that citizenship because their parents later became foreign citizens while they were minors.

For thousands of people whose citizenship applications were rejected on that basis, the decision could provide a pathway back.

A second chance for those already rejected

Italy's interior ministry has since issued a letter instructing authorities to follow the Supreme Court's interpretation.

It also provides a mechanism for people whose applications were rejected because of the minor issue to request their original applications be reconsidered, rather than starting the process again.

Fiorino says he has already seen the consequences of this play out.

One of his clients was recently denied citizenship after the consulate rejected her application because of the minor issue while the Supreme Court case was still pending.

He is now preparing a request for her application to be reviewed under the new interpretation.

"I think in a few weeks they will know the outcome," he said.

But there is an important catch.

The new pathway does not mean everyone affected by the minor issue automatically becomes an Italian citizen.

What does it mean for Ophelia?

Bryant's situation is more complicated because she never actually lodged an application.

Having spent more than two years trying to secure an appointment with the Italian consulate in Melbourne, she told SBS News that she repeatedly found that no appointments were available.

She also said she came to believe she was ineligible under the minor issue and therefore never formally submitted a claim.

That means she cannot simply ask the consulate to reopen a rejected application.

Fiorino said people in her position will need to apply under the current rules and have their individual circumstances assessed.

"The minor issue aspects may not affect, in this situation, her position, because it's been sorted out from the [Italian] Supreme Court," he said.

But other criteria introduced under Italy's separate 2025 citizenship reforms may still apply.

For Bryant, that distinction is frustrating.

"I think the way the law is going, I think Italy would recognise the claim," she said.

"But it is a question of how you get the claim in."

Administrative barriers

The legal victory could also create a new administrative challenge.

Fiorino said consulates are likely to face a significant increase in requests for reviews, while demand for new citizenship applications is already high.

From 2027, Italy's new system will also change how citizenship applications are processed, with applications ultimately being handled through a central office in Italy, he said.

For Bryant, the prospect of another bureaucratic hurdle is daunting.

"If you can't get an appointment at the embassy, how can you even get the ball rolling?," she said.

Italy has remained a constant in her life, with Bryant returning more than a dozen times to visit relatives and reconnect with her family roots. Source: Supplied / Ophelia Bryant

She has already collected certified copies of Italian family birth records, travelled repeatedly to Italy and researched her family history.

She will return again in September and is considering seeking further legal advice while she is there.

'I'm actually joining the circle'

After years of uncertainty, the ruling has renewed Bryant's hope that she may still be recognised as an Italian citizen.

When she first heard the minor issue had been overturned, she said she was "blown away".

For Bryant, Italian citizenship is not about rejecting Australia, a country she said gave her family the opportunity for a fresh start.

Instead, she said formal recognition of her Italian citizenship would connect her with the history they left behind, and the heritage she has maintained throughout her life.

"It would sort of validate that I am in fact Italian," she said.

And after years of believing the legal door was closed, she is prepared to try again.

title: Deluge at Tokyo airport kills four and strands 7,000 as Hawaii braces for tropical storm
text:
In brief Major highways in Chiba, including routes linking Narita airport with central Tokyo, remained closed.

Tropical Storm Lala is set to lash Hawaii, whose last tropical storm was in 2018.

Record ‌rainfall has left thousands of travellers stranded at Tokyo's Narita airport as ‌flooding disrupted transport, knocked out power and claimed at least four lives.

More than 360mm of rain fell in the 24 hours to Friday in parts of Chiba prefecture, which adjoins the capital ‌Tokyo, inundating roads ‌and railways. The heavy rain caused power outages to nearly 25,000 households during one of Japan's busiest holiday weeks.

Authorities said four deaths have been confirmed, including at least one person who had been trapped in a submerged vehicle.

Soldiers have been dispatched to the area to help with relief efforts.

"This case ⁠was an extremely unusual situation, even ‌by Japan's historical weather standards," Chiba governor Toshihito Kumagai told reporters on Friday.

"I have responded to many ‌disasters in the past, but I have never experienced a case like this."

The transport disruption left around 7,000 people stranded at Narita airport, an airport spokesperson said, adding that all flights are scheduled to operate normally on Friday. Japan Airlines said some flights may experience delays but ‌no cancellations are currently expected.

Major highways in Chiba, including routes linking Narita airport, one of Japan's main international transport hubs, with central Tokyo, remained closed, forcing drivers onto alternative routes and causing heavy traffic, according to highway operator NEXCO East.

Several rail services remained suspended on Friday morning, though some trains connecting Narita ⁠to Tokyo had resumed operations.

Pacific weather mayhem

Elsewhere in the Pacific, Hawaii has declared a state of emergency on Friday as it prepared for Tropical Storm Lala, which could bring powerful winds, flooding and landslides this weekend.

The Pacific storm is gaining strength according to the United States' National Weather Service, which expects it to become a hurricane as it approaches.

Winds were blowing at around 80km/h and the storm could dump up to 63.5 cm of rain in parts of the Hawaii, the weather service added.

Governor Josh Green declared a state of emergency in response to the threat, an administrative measure that frees up funds, resources and personnel in the event of damage.

"Tropical Storm Lala poses a serious threat to our state, particularly Hawaii Island — and we are taking action now to ensure resources are available where they are needed," he said.

With 210,000 residents, Hawaii Island is the archipelago's second-most populous island, far behind Oahu, which is home to more than one million people.

READ MORE Thousands of hectares burnt as El Niño intensifies Indonesia's dry season

The storm's path remains uncertain, but it is expected to remain offshore.

The last tropical storm to directly strike the archipelago was in 2018.

El Niño, a weather phenomenon that is particularly strong this year, is warming the equatorial Pacific and increasing the likelihood of cyclones. Meteorologists expect a much more active-than-average hurricane season in the region.

Scientists regularly warn that climate change, caused by humanity's burning of fossil fuels, is increasing the frequency and intensity of extreme weather events.

Tesla’s Semi has screens on either side of the steering wheel that provide a view of the traffic around the vehicle The New York Times It found the recent surge in diesel prices caused by the US war against Iran had highlighted the importance of the trucking sector moving towards electric vehicles that would both reduce operational costs, cut noise and enable the more efficient delivery of goods around the country while also reducing greenhouse gas emissions. Australia’s productivity levels have been stagnant this decade, contributing to a drop in living standards. The government announced a $10 billion productivity package in the budget, which included a range of measures including cuts to red tape aimed at small businesses, the axing of 497 nuisance tariffs and plans to reduce heavy transport costs.

The Productivity Commission report said the heavy vehicle transport sector accounted for 5 per cent of GDP, directly employed 273,000 people and was pivotal to the day-to-day functioning of the economy. The commission found that while heavier loads would do more damage to roads, the financial benefits would outweigh repair costs.

In some local government areas, for instance, internal combustion engine trucks are prevented from delivering goods to supermarkets between 10pm and 6am. title: Peter paid $2.1m for a Sydney substation. A council error has cost him $800,000
text:

NationalNSWCity life Peter paid $2.1m for a Sydney substation. A council error has cost him $800,000 David Barwell August 17, 2026 — 11:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

An inner west property owner says an error by his local council has left him facing financial ruin after he purchased a historic Newtown electricity substation that was incorrectly listed in official planning documents as free from heritage constraints. When Peter Mistrevski bought the decommissioned 1931 brick substation on Probert Street in July last year, he believed he had found a rare foothold in Sydney’s property market and an opportunity to convert the site into two homes, living in one and selling the other. Peter Mistrevski, pictured outside the substation in Newtown. Sam Mooy Before committing to the purchase, Mistrevski obtained a planning certificate from Inner West Council in March 2025 stating the property was not a heritage item, was not within a heritage conservation area and could be redeveloped under the complying development pathway, avoiding the need for a full development application. He said he relied on that certificate, seen by this publication, having it reviewed by his lawyer, architect and town planner as part of his pre-purchase due diligence. He bought the property for $2.1 million at auction.

Advertisement

“I got all the right advice. The planning certificate showed it wasn’t heritage, my town planner and architect looked at it, so I was full steam ahead,” Mistrevski said. But shortly after dotted lines on contracts were signed, a second planning certificate issued by the council in October 2025 identified the property as a heritage-listed building located within a heritage conservation area that could not be redesigned or developed under the same complying development pathway Mistrevski had planned to pursue. Mistrevski bought the property in July last year. Sam Mooy The listing effectively halted the proposed development and plunged the site into planning and legal uncertainty which Mistrevski says is now costing him $12,000 a month in holding fees, while an independent valuation has put the property at $1.3 million – $800,000 below what he paid. “The council made a massive mistake on an official document which I relied on to buy the property,” he said.

Advertisement

“I’m now unable to touch the property, modify it, I can’t live in it. It’s sending me bankrupt and [every] dollar I make is going towards the mortgage to keep the bank from repossessing it. “I tried to make lemonade and I’ve been left with a lemon.” The interior of the building. Sam Mooy The dispute is particularly fraught due to the former utility building’s history, with records showing it was constructed in 1931 during a period when substations were built across Sydney to power homes and businesses as the city grew. In recent years, decommissioned substations have attracted renewed interest from buyers seeking redevelopment opportunities in land-constrained parts of the city, with some small sites selling for more than $2 million despite the planning complexities they can present.

Advertisement

Mistrevski said the heritage listing forced him to redesign his original proposal. A development application lodged at the council in March now proposes retaining the existing substation and constructing a two-storey home behind it. But he said heritage restrictions had significantly increased costs, with planning and development expenses rising from about $50,000 to $150,000 because of the need to engage specialist heritage consultants on the revised plans. A concept image of Mistrevski’s current development plan for the site which proposes a two-storey home at the rear of the property. The application has also undergone multiple revisions in response to council concerns over the scale and bulk of the proposals and its impact on the character of the substation. More than a year after the purchase, the council has yet to determine the application. The dispute has escalated into a compensation claim against the council, with Mistrevski’s lawyers alleging the incorrect planning certificate caused substantial financial losses, including the reduction in the property’s value and lost development opportunities.

Advertisement

An Inner West Council spokesman said it could not comment on the planning certificate because the matter was subject to legal proceedings. “The development application is currently being assessed and all normal processes are being followed,” he said. Mistrevski outside the substation which dates back to 1931. Sam Mooy “More broadly, council is committed to balancing housing needs with protecting heritage.” Mistrevski said the 12-month ordeal had exposed the risks buyers face when relying on official planning information and argued purchasers should be able to have confidence in the accuracy of council-issued documents before committing to major property purchases.

“Buying a home is the biggest financial commitment most people will ever make and I feel like I’m being punished for a mistake I didn’t make,” he said. “All I’m asking for is a fair go.” Be the first to know when major news happens. title: Spruiker or the best coach? Essendon’s coaching decision looms
text:

SportAFLAFL 2026 Spruiker or the best coach? Essendon’s coaching decision looms Peter Ryan August 17, 2026 — 11:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The top 10 is locked in. Josh Fraser is short odds to coach Carlton in 2027. The big question this week is who will coach Essendon next year? Mark McVeigh coached against his former club and potential future employers on Sunday. Getty Images Whether it is announced before the Bombers’ wretched season is over or after Dean Solomon’s time as interim coach ends remains to be seen, too. It’s impossible to get a direct answer on that from anyone connected to the decision at the club. Regardless of who is asked they maintain the stance that the selection panel is still contemplating whether to recommend that the board give the job to Fremantle’s Jaymie Graham or Adelaide’s Murray Davis or a former Bomber in James Hird or Mark McVeigh.

Advertisement

The fact club president Andrew Welsh is overseas on business may have something to do with the timing, but he is due back this week. The pundits expect McVeigh to win the job based on snippets of information rather than solid evidence, but until that news breaks – which could be any time from now on – uncertainty will prevail. There is speculation that conversations have been happening about whether there could be a role to interest Hird if he did not become senior coach, but he has been on record that he started the process solely to become the senior coach. Essendon’s rooms after the loss to Sydney on Sunday were less gloomy than one might have expected given the result. The time for devastation had well passed. To the seven players with fewer than 20 games’ experience, the adventure that is AFL football remains just that. James Hird and Dean Solomon speak with then Giants interim coach Mark McVeigh during the 2022 season. Getty Images

Advertisement

Solomon says he has no idea when the decision will be announced. His only focus is preparing the team to defeat Port Adelaide on Sunday in the final round at Marvel Stadium to honour captain Andrew McGrath’s 200th game milestone. He wants to win regardless of the fact a third win of the season would likely be a farewell gift to the Tigers as it will – assuming Richmond lose to Geelong – lift Essendon off the bottom of the ladder and give the men from Punt Road first pick in the national draft. “If it is this week or next week [the coaching appointment] won’t be a distraction,” Solomon said. “We are really clear on what this week needs to look like, and the players are going to lead a lot of that.” Loading

Advertisement

The interim coach is a fighter who earned his reputation as a straight-ahead backman when the Bombers were great back in the early part of the century. The president, Welsh, was his teammate for much of that time. Although Welsh didn’t play in a flag, he believes in the Bombers as much as Solomon. That era seems a long time ago now (and it is), forcing Solomon to literally use the word “plead” when asking for the Bombers’ faithful to turn up for the final round after just 24,767 spectators turned up to the MCG on Sunday, the club’s lowest crowd at the venue since 1993. “It’s really disappointing to see our crowds down. This is the Essendon Football Club and the members and supporters have been through a lot, but this is where we dig in, we support each other and we stay tight. We wade through the swamp together in the tough times, and then we all get to celebrate the good times ahead together,” he said. The words were a sign that Solomon believes that whoever wins the coaching gig will need to reclaim the faith of a frustrated group of supporters, who have not seen a win at the MCG since the middle of last season. Dockers assistant Jaymie Graham is a candidate for the Essendon job. Getty Images

Advertisement

Of course, winning will make the most significant difference, which is why choosing the best coach will be more critical than giving the title to a spruiker. Sydney don’t need to sell. title: Grave fears longstanding Aussie job to be latest victim of cost-cutting trend: 'Very worried'
text:
A major change could soon transform Australia's public libraries, with fears that thousands of librarian jobs could disappear as councils look beyond traditional services with automated, staff-free branches.

At Wyndham City Council on the southwest outskirts of Melbourne, librarians are opposing the move to a model called "Open Libraries".

One of the City's more than 120 Wyndham City librarians told Yahoo News they are devastated that their employer is "devaluing" their profession by suggesting libraries can function without librarians.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"The fact of the matter is that our jobs are shaky at the best of times," the librarian who asked to remain anonymous said. "Be it this year or in 10 years, we're constantly fighting for funding.

"I think we're all very worried, not only that we'll lose our jobs, but that, even if we keep them, they're going to look very different to the jobs we love so much."

It comes as organisations increasingly seek ways to cut costs by replacing human jobs with technology. Gold Coast City Council recently sparked controversy for licence plate recognition vehicles to make parking enforcement more efficient.

What is an open library?

Wyndham City is one of Victoria's fastest-growing regions, and its council said it is "exploring" a model to extend opening hours beyond those staffed.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

The council claims it's meant to "complement existing staffed library services". It has heard from residents who are interested in longer library opening hours.

However, more than 5,000 people have signed a petition, reportedly including more than 90 per cent of Wyndham librarians, to push back against the model aimed at giving residents more access to community buildings, which would also reduce access to important library services.

The petition alleges that unstaffed library hours are being pitched as an enhancement to existing library services at a fraction of the cost compared to extending staffed hours.

Is your local library changing? Contact

Librarians and locals are protesting a push by one Aussie council and are worried about job security and resident safety. Source: Supplied

Library user and petition organiser Emily Brown agrees residents have been pleading for greater access to library services, but said unstaffed opening hours are "not what we're asking for".

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"We want extended opening hours with librarians, because they are part of library access," she said.

"A library is not just an open building with books in them."

RELATED:

Librarians say they are more like social workers

A librarian who spoke to Yahoo News said the planned model reflects a lack of understanding of what librarians' jobs entail. Adding, their work goes beyond shelving books and lending them out.

"The problem is if you think that a library is just about books, that means you've lived an extremely privileged life, because the library serves the most vulnerable people in our society," they said.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"We're closer to social workers these days than we are to book sellers.

"We're more likely on a normal day to help someone who's experiencing homelessness than we are to help someone choose a book to read."

Emily said it's become far more common for residents to need help navigating online forms, government services, and technology.

Proposed model criticised for alleged inequity

Access to an open library model means facilities will be available only to those over 18 who have completed a safety induction and have an additional membership option. Parents and guardians can bring children and young adults.

However, the librarian said the proposal eliminates the possibility for others to access those same services.

Regular library user, Emily Brown, said the open library model is not what residents asked for when they said they wanted extended hours. Source: Supplied

Without librarians present, it is also raising concerns about safety during unstaffed hours for people vulnerable to violence such as women, LGBTQ+ individuals, and racialised people.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Emily and the librarian have both said there has been a lack of consultation from the council regarding the potential implementation of the model.

The council said it is in the early stages of developing an approach for Wyndham and has yet to determine whether, if or where, it will implement the model. It said it would provide opportunities for the public to give feedback "once a proposed approach has been developed".

Will open libraries spread across the country?

The librarians said the model is "definitely" one they worry will spread further throughout the country, as several councils within Victoria have already moved towards open libraries.

The model has already been implemented in other council regions in Victoria, extending hours from 8.00am to 10.00pm, seven days a week. Wyndham libraries are often open between 9.00am to 8.00pm, or 10.00am to 4.00pm.
